passages.text: The question: What is Existence? What exists? Does what exists begin at some time? Does the individual self (jeevan) begin or end with the body? Is the world finally real?

This study examines those questions in Madhyasth Darshan (Co-existentialism), as presented by Shri A. Nagraj, and compares its answers with Advaita Vedanta and selected modern philosophical and scientific approaches to physical reality, consciousness, and selfhood. The core claim about time is stated in §1.4 — that kaal is duration of unit-activity and satta is timeless as ground; full treatment of time (kaal), trikaalabadh, and spacetime physics is in Nature of Time.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1. The Madhyasth Darshan Answer

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan holds that existence is coexistence: the eternal, inseparable presence of formless Omnipresence (satta) and countless formful units of nature. The units are insentient and sentient, bounded and active, while Omnipresence is all-pervasive, non-transforming, and without activity of its own. Neither is produced from the other. Units do not first exist independently and later enter coexistence; they are present only as nature saturated in Omnipresence.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: A unit becomes known through its form, its effects on other units, and its participation in an ordered whole. The same account connects the composition of the natural world with sentient life and the human capacity to understand and live in coexistence.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.1 Coexistence: Omnipresence and units

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Omnipresence is formless, all-pervasive, transparent, permeating, non-transforming, and immeasurable. It permeates every insentient and sentient unit (paragami) and is transparent in their mutuality (paradarshi), where units are imaged and recognised (MVD p. 32). These features describe one indivisible reality. Because it permeates a unit throughout, dividing that unit leaves every part within the same pervasive reality.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Omnipresence is also named Uniform Energy (sam-urja), Space, Knowledge, Consciousness, Absolute Energy, and Light (jyoti). These names describe the same pervasive reality through different relations. The name jyoti connects Omnipresence with the eternal light of realisation in it (PS pp. 80, 137). It remains actionless and without motion, wave, or pressure. Knowing, believing, and realising belong to sentient units, called jeevan.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Nature is present as countless formful units within Omnipresence. Every unit is bounded from six directions and remains saturated in the pervasive reality. Units are distinct from one another by their boundaries, not by separation from Omnipresence. What appears as empty distance between units is the same pervasive reality in which both are present. Omnipresence has no absent place, including where no local unit is perceived.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The atom is the root unit, constituted by a nucleus and particles in orbits. At larger scales, atoms compose molecules, cells, bodies, and planets. Such an organised whole is a composite unit while its definite composition and conduct persist. When it disintegrates, that composite form ends and its constituents enter other relations.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Omnipresence is state-complete: it remains unchanged. Nature is state-dynamic: units remain active, and material configurations combine and separate. Change belongs to units and their configurations within perpetual coexistence.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.2 Saturation: the ground–unit bond

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The inseparability of Omnipresence and nature is called saturation (sampriktata): every unit is soaked, submerged, and surrounded in the pervasive reality. Picture a cloth immersed in water: water is within it, it is submerged, and water surrounds it on every side. The image helps distinguish the three relations. Saturation itself is the ever-present way a unit exists in formless Omnipresence.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Because Omnipresence permeates every unit, every fragment remains saturated however often a unit is divided. Madhyasth Darshan connects this inseparability with its claim that what exists is not annihilated (SB p. 57). Division changes the configuration while leaving existent constituents. The evidential reach of this argument is examined in §6.2.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Being soaked means that every unit is endowed with energy and force. Being submerged means that it is active and stands in mutual recognition with other units. Being surrounded means that it remains regulated in definite relations. These are inseparable aspects of the unit’s presence in Omnipresence (SB p. 57; PS p. 114).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: A unit is always active and endowed with the energy evident in its activity. It bears force in state and expresses relative power in motion. Recognition and fulfilment become evident in its interactions according to its constitution and order. Saturation, energy, force, recognition, and participation in orderliness thus describe connected features of its continuing existence (SB pp. 57–62, 69).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Absolute energy (nirpeksha urja) names the pervasive reality in which units are active. Relative energy (sapeksh urja) becomes evident through their mutuality, including pressure, waves, effects, heat, sound, and electricity (MVD p. 40). This is the source’s ontological distinction; its relation to measured physical quantities and forces requires the further comparison in §6.2.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Every unit is manifest (prakashman) through its saturation in Omnipresence. The permeation of units by this state-complete reality grounds their force-endowment, activeness, and manifestness (AVD pp. 115–116; SB p. 248). Thus the unit’s manifest presence among other units belongs to its inseparable bond with Omnipresence. In mutual facing, units are imaged to one another, and imaging provides the basis of mutual recognition (PS p. 121; SB pp. 248–251). The same inseparable coexistence is considered here through the unit’s saturation and through its manifestation in mutuality.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: In insentient nature, recognition takes the form of definite responsiveness. An atomic particle recognises another according to constitution, distance, force, and relation; fulfilment is the resulting definite conduct. Heat accepted and redistributed by matter, particles maintaining definite distances in an atom, and atoms combining in definite ways illustrate this responsiveness. Imaging supplies the accompanying account of how units are manifest to one another.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Activity includes effort, motion, and result together: effort as active tendency, motion as its state of change, and result as the condition attained. Every physical and chemical activity bears all three. Force is recognised in state and power in motion; relative energy becomes evident through the mutuality of units.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Being surrounded in Omnipresence establishes regulation. Units remain regulated and conserved through their mediative organisation. In an atom, the nucleus mediates generative and degenerative tendencies and regulates relative powers. This regulation becomes evident as law and definite conduct (§1.6.1).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Nature saturated in Omnipresence is also called knowledge: coexistence itself is the complete content available to be known. Units are manifest within it; understanding that content is an activity of jeevan. Existence is therefore intelligible and available for study.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.3 The unit and its four aspects in mutuality

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Every unit is manifest (prakashman) with four inseparable aspects: form (roop), properties (guna), essential nature (svabhav), and dharma (PS p. 119). Form is shape, volume, and density: the real framework by which a unit is bounded and individuated. The unit in its constituted configuration is the bimb; its image in mutual facing is pratibimb, and its being imaged is pratibimban (PS pp. 121, 135; SB pp. 249–250). What is imaged is a real unit with its own form.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Properties (guna) are the relative powers of a unit, inseparable from the unit that bears them (guni). They produce generative, degenerative, or mediative effects when units interact. Essential nature (svabhav) is the usefulness or characteristic contribution of those effects in a given order and context. Dharma is innateness: what is inseparable from the unit and fulfilled in its activity. Existence is common to all orders; growth, hope to live, and happiness are added cumulatively in the higher orders.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: In the mutuality of units, light (prakash) also names imaging: a unit’s imaging is prakash, and units remain imaged on all sides (MVD p. 45; PS pp. 119, 121). In mutual facing, imaging is the basis of recognition and is indispensable for units’ becoming manifest to one another. This includes insentient units; imaging is an existential relationship before it becomes a subject of human perception or understanding. The same unit bears all four aspects, while the recognition and evaluation of those aspects take the forms available in each order (SB pp. 248–252).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Imaging and influence have distinct roles in this mutuality. Through imaging a unit is manifest to another; through its relative powers it exerts effects. Both belong to the account of insentient nature. In animal living, recognition of essential nature becomes evident in friendliness and opposition; in human mutuality, essential natures are exchanged as values and dharma is evaluated as resolution (SB pp. 249–252). The whole unit’s manifestness supplies what is to be understood, while human understanding of it requires the knowing activities of jeevan. Its image alone does not constitute that completed understanding.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The peepal tree illustrates the four aspects:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Aspect Peepal-tree example Form (roop) A bounded biological composition with roots, trunk, branches, leaves, fruit, and seeds. The constituted tree is the bimb, imaged in mutual facing as pratibimb. Property (guna) Relative powers become effective in mutuality: a seed in conducive soil, water, and climate participates in growth; disintegration changes the effects its constituents exert. Essential nature (svabhav) Effects are vitalising or devitalising according to the affected body and conditions. Their usefulness is definite in that mutuality. Dharma Existence and growth. The living tree grows and produces seeds that carry its composition method forward.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Every entity’s characteristic contribution is manifest, communicated, and expressed according to its state, motion, developmental standing, and order (SB p. 179). Presentation (prakashan), communication (sampreshana), and expression (abhivyakti) are connected aspects of this manifestness. In insentient nature, they concern the unit’s manifest form, properties, and participation in mutuality. Sentient jeevan manifests and communicates through a body, while its inexhaustible forces and powers are active and manifest through its inward and outward activities (SB pp. 52, 63). During human awakening progression, communicating and expressing capacity, ability, and receptivity are themselves aspects of manifestness (SB p. 66). Their fulfilment in awakened living carries understood coexistence into speech, work, and behaviour (§1.14).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Atomic constitution and motion-path differentiate a unit’s form and the capacities through which its relative powers operate. Atomic kind, state, and measure vary with nuclear and orbital particle constitution. As a developing atom changes constitution, its form and properties change. Structure therefore bears and constrains what the unit can express.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Those capacities become effective in definite mutualities. Guna concerns the effect when units come together, svabhav its usefulness, and dharma the unit’s innateness and fulfilment. Understanding a unit therefore includes both its constituted form and its relations with other units.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Given the participating units, their constitutions, state, motion, distance, and environment, insentient effects and conduct are definite. Different mutualities yield different definite effects. In human living, understanding and evaluation additionally guide how relationships are fulfilled.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Each unit is a whole along with its environment. It retains its constitution and capacities while participating in definite mutualities. Its characteristic identity in orderliness—its own “ness”—is expressed through its images, effects, and usefulness to others (SB pp. 51, 250).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The four aspects also describe the unit’s activity. Effort is associated with dharma and essential nature; motion with essential nature and properties; result with form and, in the completeness account, immortality (SB pp. 60–62). The overlap matters: essential nature concerns both effort and motion. These are interconnected descriptions of an active unit, whose developmental goals are explained through constitutional, activity, and conduct completeness (§§1.7.1, 1.11).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Truth of a unit is stated in three complementary aspects (SB pp. 250–251; MVD pp. 88, 97; YAT). Inherent truth (vastugat satya) is the unit’s own form, properties, essential nature, and innateness. Positional truth (vastu-sthiti satya) is that same unit in place, time, and direction—its mutuality with other units. Existential truth (sthiti satya) is nature saturated in Omnipresence: coexistence as the standing condition that is not itself timed. Knowing a unit completely means knowing what it is, how it stands among others, and that it exists in the pervasive ground.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: In the natural state, a unit’s activity accords with its innateness and definite conduct. In the excited state, pressure from a mutuality displaces its activity from that accord and carries the possibility of decline. In physicochemical exchange, units give and take and then reinstate natural-state motion. Development means movement toward fuller order-definite expression; decline means movement away from it. Units participate according to their constitution and order; some developing atoms attain constitutional completeness.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: At the human order, definite bodily composition is not sufficient for humane conduct; knowing and believing must guide recognition, evaluation, and fulfilment.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.4 Time, causation, conservation, and the perpetual world

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Time is the reckoning of the duration of activity (SB p. 251). Recurrent activities provide its measures. Omnipresence, being without transformation, is not temporal in the sense in which unit-activity is measured; units and configurations undergo the changes through which duration is recognised.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Omnipresence is supreme cause (mahakaran) in the sustaining sense: every activity exists as nature saturated in it. Particular transformations occur through active units in mutuality. Composition, decomposition, and development belong to units, while the pervasive ground remains unchanged.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Existence is perpetual. Omnipresence and the underlying reality (vastu) of units neither arise from non-being nor pass into non-being. Form (roop), composition, and association change while the realities participating in change remain. Thus the decomposition of a compound or body ends that organisation while its constituents continue. “Brahma is truth, the world is perpetual” affirms both the pervasive ground and the reality of the changing world.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: General indestructibility concerns what persists through changing configurations. The persistence of one organised individual requires a further account of its constitution; Madhyasth Darshan supplies that account for jeevan through constitutional completeness (§1.7.1).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.5 Composition: atoms, molecules, and bodies

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: There is a natural inclination toward coexistence throughout nature. Atomic particles assemble into atoms, atoms into molecules, and molecules into molecular forms. Compositional progression becomes evident in chemical substances, biological cells, vegetation, animal bodies, and the human body. Each level depends on definite composition method and conducive environment.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Composition retains a dependence on its constituents: iron objects remain iron, and bodies built from biological (pranic) cells remain pranic compositions. Material composition can manifest as the pranic order and return to material constituents through disintegration (SB pp. 75–77). These changes supply bodies and environments, including the human body. Development within an atom is the further line through which sentient jeevan becomes possible (§1.7.1).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Mixtures and compounds should be distinguished. In a mixture, components retain their respective conducts. In a compound, components combine in definite proportion and establish a new bounded unit with a new constitution, relational capacities, and order-specific conduct. Biological composition transmits its method through seed and lineage. Bodies in animal and human orders are species-conformant compositions built from pranic cells; their sentience belongs to the jeevan joined with the body, not to composition alone.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.6 The four orders of nature

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Nature is organised into four orders: material, bio or pranic, animal, and knowledge or human. Higher-order bodies contain and organise material and pranic compositions, thereby evidencing existence and growth. In the animal and knowledge orders, hope to live and happiness belong to the jeevan–body joint form: the body provides the expression medium, while the further dharma is attributed to jeevan. The higher orders therefore include the lower-order dharmas while adding a further dharma and a distinctive mode in which essential nature is expressed.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Order Principal manifestation Order-specific expression of essential nature Dharma, cumulatively stated Material (padarth-avastha) Atoms, molecules, physical and chemical compositions integration–disintegration existence Bio (pranic; pran-avastha) Biological cells, vegetation, bodily composition vitalising–devitalising existence and growth Animal (jeeva-avastha) Body–jeevan joint form under species-conformance cruel–uncruel existence, growth, and hope to live Knowledge (human; gyan-avastha) Human body–jeevan joint form with knowing and believing fortitude, courage, generosity, kindness, grace, compassion existence, growth, hope to live, and happiness

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Integration and disintegration name effects among material constituents. Vitalising and devitalising name whether a biological or chemical composition supports or obstructs bodily nourishment and protection in the relevant context. Cruelty is intrinsically relational because it means causing suffering to another; non-cruelty is its order-specific complement. Humane essential nature is evidenced through qualities fulfilled in behaviour and relationship. These are definite forms of participation, although the human can misrecognise or fail to fulfil them under delusion.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The material and bio orders are insentient. The animal and knowledge orders are joint expressions of an insentient body and a sentient unit, jeevan. Hope to live is the animal-order dharma, expressed through the sentient unit. The animal body provides for hope-bound, species-conformant expression; the human body provides for imagination, freedom of action, knowing, believing, and the full possibility of awakening. The bodily-medium distinction is developed in §1.8. Happiness is the human dharma because the human seeks not merely continued living but resolution and the continuity of happiness.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The five koshas describe capacities distributed across these orders. Material nature is described through annamaya and pranamaya; pranic nature adds manomaya, the selective reception of nourishment. Animal and deluded human living include anandamaya, the expression of happiness and unhappiness. Awakened human living includes vigyanmaya, the capacity to receive essential knowledge (MVD pp. 49–50). This classification begins with material nature. It therefore differs both from the five faculties of jeevan (§1.8) and from the Advaita account of five sheaths covering the Self (§2.6).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Two developmental lines therefore meet in the animal and human joint forms: compositional progression supplies the body, while development in the atom supplies constitutionally complete jeevan. Constitutional completeness and awakening are developed in §§1.7 and 1.11.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Existential progression names the order in which these manifestations become possible under conducive conditions: material, pranic, animal, and knowledge. Individual compositions participate according to their constitution and environment. Biological compositions return to material constituents when they disintegrate, while many atoms continue in physical and chemical constitution.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.6.1 Regulation, law, and conformance

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Regulation is inherent in nature saturated in Omnipresence. Orderliness is self-regulation (swatah-saspurt) in the coexisting orders. Omnipresence is the sustaining condition; the mediative nucleus regulates activities within an atom; and order-specific conformance describes the conduct evident at larger scales.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Regulation becomes evident as law because every unit has provision for recognising and fulfilling according to definite constitution. The way of existence (niyati-vidhi) names the four modes of conformance (anushangita):

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Order Conformance mode Character Material (padarth-avastha) Result- or structure-conformance (parinam-anushangita) Definite Bio (pranic; pran-avastha) Seed-conformance (beej-anushangita) Definite Animal (jeeva-avastha) Species-conformance (vansh-anushangita) Definite in body and inherited conduct-pattern Knowledge (human; gyan-avastha) Sanskar-conformance (sanskar-anushangita) Conduct follows acquired acceptances and dispositions, which may express delusion or awakening

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Animal conduct includes inherited species-patterns accepted from gestation and followed after birth. Human bodily composition also remains species-conformant, but human conduct is principally jeevan-based and sanskar-conformant. Sanskar concerns acquired acceptances and tendencies that guide conduct. Education and tradition can therefore reproduce delusion or support awakening; humane education–sanskar makes understanding and the disposition to live by it available.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.7 Two lines of development

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Compositional progression builds molecules, cells, bodies, and their environments. Development within the atom changes an atomic constitution until it becomes complete. These two lines meet in animal and human living: composition supplies the body, while a constitutionally complete sentient atom, jeevan, operates through it. The body’s organisation provides the medium through which sentient activity can be expressed.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.7.1 Constitutional completeness (T1)

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Development in the atom culminates when an evolving constitution becomes satisfied. Constitution-oriented atoms are described as hungry when they can absorb particles and undigested or overfull when they carry particles they seek to expel. Through absorption and displacement, atoms return to natural-state motion or participate in further constitution. When the particles required for a particular developing constitution are integrated, that constitution becomes complete.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Constitutional completeness is an irreversible transition. Up to that point the two kinds of change are tied together: in matter, qualitative change does not occur without quantitative change in constitution, which is why atomic kind and capacity track particle number. Completeness separates them. The particle constitution is closed: qualitative activity continues, but particles no longer increase or decrease.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The atom is then jeevan, with inexhaustible force and power expressed as hope, thought, desire, resoluteness, and evidence. It is liberated from molecular-bondage and weight-bondage and established in hope-bondage: it no longer participates as a weighable atom bound into molecular composition, while its sentient activity is organised around hope. The relation of these source categories to contemporary physical measurement remains open (§6.2.1). Constitutional completeness concerns this transition of an insentient atom into sentient status.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: T1 establishes the sentient unit with its capacity for knowing. How fully this capacity is expressed also depends on its bodily medium. Animal bodies permit hope-bound, species-conformant expression; the fully developed human nervous system provides for the complete activity of understanding. The faculties through which jeevan operates are described next.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Saturation and constitutional completeness: compositional development supplies bodies, while development in the atom reaches the constitutionally complete sentient unit jeevan; the diagram does not claim that sentience is produced by biological complexity

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: This closed constitution supplies Madhyasth Darshan’s specific account of individual persistence. The jeevan no longer gains or loses particles and remains free from molecular- and weight-bondage. The body is a decomposable pranic composition; jeevan is the sentient atom that operates through it and continues when the joint form ends.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.8 Jeevan: structure and faculties

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Jeevan is the constitutionally complete sentient atom; the body is the biological instrument through which it acts. As an illustration, the body serves as a vehicle and jeevan as its conscious driver and knower. The body supplies sense organs, the brain (medhas), and capacities for physical expression. The brain receives and translates signals between jeevan and the body. Jeevan supplies hope, thought, desire, resolve, comprehension (bodh), authenticity, and realisation. A bodily limitation constrains expression through that medium; delusion concerns how jeevan identifies itself and organises its activity.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The primary texts describe five inseparable strengths or faculties in jeevan. Atma is the nucleus; buddhi, chitta, vritti, and mun are associated with the first through fourth orbits. Each faculty’s characteristic power has paired activities in projection (paravartan) and reflection (pratyavartan) (SB p. 63).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Faculty and characteristic power Projection Reflection Mun — hope selection taste-recognition Vritti — thought analysis deliberation Chitta — desire visualisation contemplation; direct apprehension (sakshatkar) Buddhi — resoluteness (ritambhara) resolve comprehension (bodh) Atma — evidence authenticity realisation

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: These are the ten activities of jeevan. Every jeevan operates through all ten; their effective organisation and evidence in living differ. The same inexhaustible strengths and powers underlie the equal capacity of jeevan in every human (SB p. 91). Equal capacity does not imply identical present understanding or bodily ability. Projection is the outward evidencing direction: understanding is expressed through resolve, thought, selection, work, and behaviour. Reflection (pratyavartan) is the inward knowing direction: experience and study are accepted, compared, directly apprehended, comprehended, and realised.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Reflection concerns jeevan’s understanding. Imaging (pratibimban, §1.3) is a unit’s presence in mutual facing; visualisation (chitran) is an activity of chitta. At the activity level, force (bal) names activity in state and power (shakti) activity in motion. The faculty-level strengths and their characteristic powers are distinguished in the table above.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The source also places five insentient forces alongside the sentient faculties: electromagnetic force with mun, gravitational force with vritti, weak interaction with chitta, strong interaction with buddhi, and mediative force with atma (SB pp. 84–85). This is a further relation proposed by the text. Whether it is a structural analogy or a literal physical correspondence, and what evidence would establish it, requires the assessment in §6.2.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Study proceeds inward by the reflection circuit. Truth in the form of coexistence is accepted through tasting in mun, deliberated in vritti, directly apprehended (sakshatkar) through contemplation in chitta, and comprehended (bodh) in buddhi. Buddhi’s accordance with atma culminates in realisation. Projection expresses this understanding through authenticity, resolve, visualisation, analysis, and selection into living conduct.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Tasting (asvadan) at mun has sensory, value-based, and goal-based forms (ruchi-mulak, mulya-mulak, and lakshya-mulak). Sensory tasting concerns sound, touch, form, taste, and smell through the body. Value-based tasting concerns fulfilment in recognised relationships. Goal-based tasting concerns the purpose of activity; awakening makes that purpose definite as resolution, prosperity, fearlessness, and coexistence. Development changes the governing orientation from sensory attraction toward relationship-fulfilment and the human goal, so what is accepted at mun is no longer organised by bodily sensation alone.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: In animal living, the body has a brain and sensory organisation but not the fully enriched nervous system of the human body. It therefore mediates hope-bound selection, taste-recognition, and species-conformant conduct without providing for the complete evidence of understanding. This is a limitation of bodily expression, not an animal’s erroneous attempt at human evaluation.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The human body supplies the developed medium required for the full circuit, but bodily provision does not itself produce awakening. In deluded human living, jeevan identifies itself with the body and organises only four and a half activities effectively around bodily sensitivity: selection, taste, analysis, visualisation, and deliberation restricted to pleasant–unpleasant, healthy–unhealthy, and profit–loss.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Deliberation has six perspectives: pleasant–unpleasant (priya–apriya), healthy–unhealthy (hita–ahita), profit–loss (labh–alabh), justice–injustice (nyaya–anyaya), dharma–adharma, and truth–untruth (satya–asatya). Only the first three govern deliberation in deluded living; justice, dharma, and truth have yet to guide it. In this restricted sense, deliberation is called a half activity. The remaining activities are present but lack the content and coherent direction of understanding in conduct. The human recognises and fulfils sensory aims without joining them to complete knowing and believing.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The texts distinguish sensitivity (sanvedansheelta) from cognisance (sangyansheelta). Sensitivity is responsiveness through the body and senses; cognisance is jeevan’s understanding of relationship, value, and orderliness. Awakening does not eliminate sensitivity. It brings sensory recognition and fulfilment under the guidance of knowing and believing, so cognisance and sensitivity operate in balance rather than as rival capacities.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The direction of faculty regulation distinguishes stages of awakening. Higher-conformance (purvanukram) is guidance descending from atma through buddhi, chitta, and vritti to mun; lower-conformance (paranukram) is sensory drive pushing inward from the body (MVD pp. 207–208). Cognisance regulates sensitivity in the former; sensitivity organises the faculties around the body in the latter.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: In the partially awakened condition, mun and vritti are driven by chitta. In the half-awakened condition, mun, vritti, and chitta are guided by buddhi, while resolve remains without self-realisation. In awakening, atma regulates and disciplines buddhi, chitta, vritti, and mun; knowing, believing, recognising, and fulfilling become coherent. Study supplies the content of understanding; practice evidences and stabilises it in behaviour.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The seer–doer–enjoyer account describes three coordinated roles of the same jeevan: it knows, acts through work and behaviour, and undergoes the results. Under delusion, doing and undergoing continue while the seer-status remains incompletely evidenced. Awakening establishes jeevan as seer through understanding coexistence and itself as the knower; this understanding then guides doing and enjoying toward mutual satisfaction (MVD pp. 115, 288–289; KD 3.17–3.18).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.9 Jeevan harmonies and experience

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Happiness, peace, contentment, and bliss are jeevan values: harmonies between adjacent faculties, each experienced at the outer faculty of its pair. Happiness is the harmony of mun with vritti, peace of vritti with chitta, contentment of chitta with buddhi, and bliss of buddhi with atma. These are also described as four stages of happiness.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Each harmony is borne at the outer faculty of its pair: happiness at mun, peace at vritti, contentment at chitta, and bliss at buddhi (MVD pp. 328–346). For example, peace at vritti is the absence of resistance between desire and thought, the orientations of chitta and vritti. Naming its location and naming the faculties in harmony thus describe the same activity. Realisation at atma is ultimate bliss (paramanand), whose effect reaches the remaining faculties (MVD pp. 100–101).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The movement is not a sequence of temporary moods. It describes progressively complete coherence in the activity of jeevan. Curiosity in mun, enthusiasm in vritti, delight in chitta, elation and immersion in buddhi, and realisation in atma name the inward channel of energies toward awakening. Inward regulation is the discipline of the orbital faculties by mediative atma, followed by regulation of bodily activity through understanding.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The four jeevan values correspond to human goals in living:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Jeevan value Borne at Faculty harmony Human goal and field of evidence Happiness mun mun–vritti Resolution in the person Peace vritti vritti–chitta Resolution and prosperity in the family Contentment chitta chitta–buddhi Resolution, prosperity, and fearlessness in social participation Bliss buddhi buddhi–atma Resolution, prosperity, fearlessness, and coexistence in living

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The settings in which understanding is expressed and assessed widen cumulatively: family prosperity includes resolution, fearless social participation includes resolution and prosperity, and living in coexistence includes all three (KD 3.12, printed p. 112; JV p. 61). These are principal correspondences between inner harmony and living. They do not confine a value to one social setting or make a faculty pair the cause of an institution.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Happiness toward bliss: harmony within jeevan becomes evident through resolution, prosperity, fearlessness, and coexistence; this is the felt and lived expression of activity and conduct completeness, not a fourth completeness transition

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Awakening develops through repeated reflection and projection. By reflection, one understands; through projection, that understanding is made evident. Evidence widens from one issue to further issues, each accomplished understanding becoming the basis for the next projection (KD 3.12). Book knowledge alone is not the completion of this process. Study, practice, work, behaviour, result, and purpose must become coherent.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Jeevan remains active through bodily sleep and, according to MD, persists after bodily death. Its subsequent association with another body is also affirmed (JV pp. 20, 55). These claims rest on the doctrine of constitutional completeness; their relation to public evidence is considered in §6.2.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.10 Karma: desire, activity, and result

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Effort–motion–result is the structure of kriyā, or activity, throughout nature. In the sentient unit it is expressed through projection and reflection. When the human intends and acts through the body, the same structure is studied as desire, karma, and result.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Activity together with aspiration is karma; motion together with awareness is called complete activity (KD Ch. 1, printed pp. 1–2). Every karma has a result. Its five limbs are doer, cause, objective, result, and effect. These distinguish the actor, motive, intended aim, attained result, and wider consequence. The balance of desire, karma, and result is accomplishment of the desire. “Complete activity” here concerns awareness in action; completeness of understanding is developed in §1.11.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Karma is human activity under freedom of action. Deluded humans are independent while performing actions but dependent while undergoing their results. In awakened living, understanding precedes action and the attained result is evaluated and received within resolution. This is independence in both doing and undergoing: consequences remain, while their reception is free of unresolved contradiction. Living proof requires understanding to regulate conduct and complete the projection–reflection cycle.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Prarabdha names results still to be undergone when knowing, desiring, doing, and enjoying have differed (MVD p. 91). It locates unresolved consequences within this account of action and result. Advaita’s use of the term for already-begun karma sustaining embodied life after knowledge belongs to a different account (§2.9).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.11 Awakening: activity and conduct completeness

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Nature saturated in state-complete Omnipresence is oriented toward development and awakening until realisation in Omnipresence. Development in its full sense includes constitutional completeness, activity completeness, conduct completeness, and their continuity. Awakening is resolution and authenticity. This direction is fulfilled according to the constitution and order of the participating unit.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The three developmental goals are immortality of result, restfulness of effort, and destination of motion. Constitutional completeness establishes the non-decomposable constitution of jeevan. Activity completeness settles its internal search through realisation and resolution. Conduct completeness establishes its outward activity as humane conduct and participation in universal orderliness.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Transition Completeness Principal goal What is established T1 Constitutional completeness Immortality of result Constitutionally complete sentient atom, jeevan T2 Activity completeness Restfulness of effort Realisation and resolution in awakened jeevan T3 Conduct completeness Destination of motion Continuous authentic conduct, contributing to humane tradition

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Each activity includes effort, motion, and result. The three goals identify what becomes complete in constitution, understanding, and conduct: T1 establishes the persistent sentient unit, T2 settles its search through realisation, and T3 establishes continuity of that understanding in conduct (SB p. 58).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.11.1 Activity completeness (T2)

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Activity completeness is restfulness of effort. The texts define restfulness as the absence of delusion. Delusion is not absence of activity: jeevan continues hoping, thinking, desiring, acting, and undergoing results while mistaking the body for the self. The unresolved effort is the continual search for happiness without understanding jeevan, coexistence, and humane conduct well enough to guide living.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Activity completeness is attained when knowing, believing, recognising, and fulfilling become coherent through realisation. The inward knowing circuit of jeevan and the harmonies between its faculties now operate in resolution. This establishes the understanding through which the seer guides action and its results.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.11.2 Conduct completeness (T3)

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Conduct completeness is the destination of motion. Understanding becomes continuous in work, behaviour, and participation in orderliness. Reflection provides truthful understanding, and projection evidences it in living. At conduct completeness, action fulfils relationships and its result is mutual satisfaction.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: T2 concerns the settlement of jeevan’s internal activity in realisation and resolution. T3 concerns the individual’s continuous expression of that resolution in conduct. Its social fulfilment includes contributing to a humane tradition; individual and social completeness remain distinguishable (MVD pp. 15–16, 80). The human goals and social systems through which understanding is transmitted are developed in §1.15.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Two developments that must not be collapsed: compositional progression builds bodies and environments as support for jeevan; atomic development alone reaches constitutional completeness (T1) and continues through activity and conduct completeness (T2, T3)

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.12 Progressions and planes

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Four terms distinguish the order of manifestation, definite conduct, atomic development, and awakening.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.12.1 Terms for order and development

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Term Meaning Existential progression (niyati-kram) Definite order in which material, pranic, animal, and knowledge orders become manifest under appropriate conditions Way of existence (niyati-vidhi) The four conformance modes explained with the orders (§1.6.1) Development progression (vikas-kram) Physicochemical development and composition, including constitution-oriented atoms, until constitutional completeness becomes possible Awakening progression (jagriti-kram) Qualitative development within constitutionally complete jeevan toward activity and conduct completeness

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Existential progression and the way of existence describe the four orders and their conformance (§1.6). Development progression and awakening progression describe the atomic and sentient path. At the animal-order junction, compositional progression supplies the body and development in the atom supplies jeevan. In the knowledge order, the human body becomes the medium for the full awakening progression. The relation between this ontological ordering and evolutionary history is examined in §6.2.3.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.12.2 Four planes

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Order identifies the kind of manifestation; plane identifies developmental standing. The four planes are physicochemical, delusional, deific, and divine or complete.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Plane Developmental standing Physicochemical Insentient constitution and composition before constitutional completeness Delusional Sentient jeevan without realisation; in humans, body taken as self Deific Activity completeness: realisation and resolution Divine (complete) Conduct completeness: living proof and its continuity

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Orders and planes are therefore not interchangeable. The crosswalk below shows how the main classifications meet without turning them into one sequence:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Manifestation or human type Developmental source Plane and completeness Characteristic expression Material and pranic orders Physicochemical composition Physicochemical; before T1 Structure- and seed-conformance Animal joint form Animal body from composition; jeevan from T1 Constitutionally complete jeevan before awakening Hope-bound, species-conformant expression; bodily limitation is not human body-identification Animalistic-human and demonic-human Human body with deluded jeevan Delusional; T1 only Body-identification and four-and-a-half activities organised around sensitivity Humane or discerning human Awakening progression becomes established Movement from delusional toward deific; no fifth plane is added Knowing and believing increasingly guide recognition and fulfilment Deific-human Awakening progression Deific; T2 activity completeness Realisation and resolution Divine-human Continuity of awakening Divine; T3 conduct completeness Authentic conduct and living proof in tradition

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The five human types classify modes of consciousness and conduct, not biological species or fixed social classes. The traditional plane name delusional covers sentient standing before realisation, but the specific error of taking the body as self applies to humans; an animal’s narrower expression is a limitation of its bodily medium.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The completion of this development is also called padmukti, release from the planes in the divine or complete condition (SB p. 52). The term concerns freedom from incomplete developmental standing; the realised jeevan continues to exist and evidence understanding.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Four orders mapped to four planes: compositional progression supplies bodies; constitutional completeness establishes jeevan; activity and conduct completeness mark human awakening

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan architecture of coexistence: Omnipresence and units as co-eternal poles bound by saturation; four orders with material and pranic as insentient and animal and knowledge as body–jeevan joint forms; separate compositional and atomic-development lines meeting in animal and human forms; and constitutional, activity, and conduct completeness T1–T3

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.13 Values, relationships, and evaluation

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Human understanding becomes evident in the recognition and fulfilment of relationships. The values involved connect the activities of jeevan with what people do for one another and with the material means they use.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.13.1 Relationships and the thirty values

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Nothing in nature exists in isolation. Complementarity and mutual recognition are eternally present in coexistence and become evident through relationships among units. At the physical and chemical level, complementarity is expressed as definite interaction and composition. In the biological order it is expressed through nourishment, growth, seed-conformance, and the composition method of cells. In the animal order, sentient selection and taste-recognition are expressed through the limited bodily medium under species-conformance. In the knowledge order, the fully developed human bodily medium makes knowing, believing, recognising, evaluating, and fulfilling available as one coherent possibility.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: A relationship (sambandh) carries definite expectations toward completeness; a contact (sampark) involves voluntarily undertaken expectations. Both remain subject to justice and humane conduct (MVD pp. 61–62, 311–312). Parent and child exemplify a relationship whose values require recognition and fulfilment. As an illustration of contact, neighbours may choose the terms of maintaining a shared wall; those chosen terms do not make their obligation to act justly optional.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Value has order-specific expression. In its universal ontological sense, value is essentiality (maulikta) and participation in orderliness (vyavastha mein bhaagidari): the definite conduct through which a unit complements others in coexistence (SB p. 50). Usefulness (upyogita) is that essentiality as it appears in objects. Human living has four connected dimensions—realisation, thought, behaviour, and work—across which thirty core values are enumerated in five families (PS pp. 151, 154). Their definitions and connections are developed across the primary works.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Value family Principal content and field Object values Usefulness is the definite utility of a material object; art or aesthetic value (kala-mulya) adds meaningful convenience and beauty to that usefulness. Here art names a value realised in the object; kala also names the skilful activity of expression (§1.14). These are two values within one object-value family. Jeevan values Happiness, peace, contentment, and bliss name harmony within the sentient unit (§1.9). Human values Fortitude, courage, generosity, kindness, grace, and compassion: the six humane and higher-humane essential natures through which humaneness is evidenced. Established values Trust, respect, affection, care, guidance, reverence, glory, gratitude, and love become evident when human relationships are recognised and fulfilled. Expressed values (shishta-mulya) The nine corresponding powers in motion: concordance, cordiality, dedication, generosity, naturalness, devoutness, simplicity, humility, and non-otherness.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: These families are related but not interchangeable. Inner harmony, humane disposition, relationship-fulfilment, expressed conduct in relationship, and the usefulness of objects answer different evaluative questions.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Taken together, the four jeevan values, six human values, nine established values, nine expressed values, and two object values are the thirty values (tees mulya) across realisation, thought, behaviour, and work (Paribhasha, pp. 151, 154). The nine established values in state are paired with the nine expressed values in motion: trust with concordance, respect with cordiality, affection with dedication, care with generosity, guidance with naturalness, reverence with devoutness, glory with simplicity, gratitude with humility, and love with non-otherness (vishwas–saujanyata, samman–sauhardta, sneha–nishtha, mamta–udarta, vatsalya–sahajta, shraddha–pujyata, gaurav–saralta, kritagyata–saumyata, prem–ananyata).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Object values belong to material units and become evident in their usefulness. The other four families concern activities of jeevan. Named values are also located at particular faculties and paired with the expressions through which they are carried outward (MVD pp. 328–348; AVD pp. 91–94).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The four jeevan values are harmonies between adjacent faculties, experienced respectively at mun, vritti, chitta, and buddhi (§1.9). The nine established values are borne three each at chitta, vritti, and mun, with their corresponding expressed values. The humane essential natures are named at vritti and mun, some at positions of their own and some as the expression paired with another value. The family identifies the evaluative role a value fulfils; the faculty identifies where that activity occurs in jeevan. Neither classification replaces the other.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Bearing a value and evidencing it remain distinct. Values are recognised and fulfilled in relationship, and where relationships are not recognised they do not flow (JV, p. 55). The faculty account states what a named value is and where it is borne; the evaluative account of §1.13.3 states how its fulfilment is judged. The full enumeration and its unresolved readings are set out in The Sixty-One Activity Pairs of Jeevan, and the value families are developed in Axiology: Value Theory §§1.1–1.3.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Recognition and fulfilment are definite below the knowledge order according to structural, seed, and species conformance. Animals do not fail to perform a human evaluation; their narrower expression follows from the bodily medium described in §1.8. Human evaluation can succeed or fail because freedom of action operates while knowing and believing may remain disconnected from recognition and fulfilment. Inherent provision still requires conducive conditions: a seed germinates in a suitable environment, and the human possibility of awakening requires an environment in which understanding can be studied, practised, and evidenced.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.13.2 Evaluative perspectives and justice

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Recognition and selection occur before the knowledge order. In animal expression, jeevan selects and recognises taste through hope-bound activity mediated by the animal body. The human distinction is explicit evaluation through six perspectives and the capacity to evaluate relationships, values, justice, dharma, and truth through knowing and believing, then to reorganise conduct accordingly. A unit’s manifestness and imaging provide a basis of recognition; human evaluation additionally requires understanding what is recognised. Error enters when deluded jeevan evaluates from body-identification and treats sensory, bodily, or material criteria as exhaustive.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Human behaviour is expressed through six perspectives: pleasant–unpleasant, healthy–unhealthy, profit–loss, justice–injustice, dharma–adharma, and truth–untruth.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Perspective Principal domain Place in humane evaluation Pleasant–unpleasant Sensation and instinct Necessary but insufficient as organising standpoint Healthy–unhealthy Body Necessary but insufficient as organising standpoint Profit–loss Material production and exchange Necessary but insufficient as organising standpoint Justice–injustice Human relationship and behaviour Humane regulation of conduct Dharma–adharma Thought and resolution Humane regulation of thought Truth–untruth Existence as coexistence Ground of realisation and knowledge

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The first three perspectives are not rejected in their proper domains. Food may be pleasant, bodily activity healthy, and production materially beneficial. Delusion occurs when these become the final refuge and overrule justice, resolution, and truth. Humane perspective subordinates sensory, bodily, and material aims to justice, dharma, and truth.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Unit dharma—the inseparable innateness of a unit—must be distinguished from the dharma–adharma perspective. The latter evaluates whether thought and policy support resolution and overall orderliness. Similarly, justice is both a perspective by which conduct is assessed and the name of a completed relational activity.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.13.3 The dual role of justice

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: As a perspective, justice evaluates behaviour as just or unjust. As completed relational activity, justice is recognising relationships, fulfilling values, evaluating the fulfilment, and achieving mutual satisfaction. Trust, respect, affection, and other relationship values contribute to justice but are not individually identical with it.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Humane conduct brings together value, character, and ethics (mulya–charitra–naitikta). Values supply the content to be fulfilled; character concerns definite conduct; ethics concerns the policies by which humaneness is protected and supported (Paribhasha, p. 151). Bearing values in jeevan does not by itself ensure their fulfilment: a relationship must be recognised and its responsibilities carried out (JV p. 55).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Consider a person caring for an ill parent. Recognising the relationship, understanding the parent’s needs, arranging suitable care, and checking whether it has helped distinguish knowing from fulfilment and evaluation. A kind intention alone does not establish adequate care. Nor does purchasing a useful object complete the relationship: the object supports bodily need, while attention, trust, respect, and care concern how the people relate. The example connects the unit’s useful capacity, the caregiver’s understanding, and the test of mutual satisfaction.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Law applies across the four orders as definite regulation. In human living, regulation and balance are fulfilled as justice in behaviour, resolved thought as dharma, and realisation in truth as coexistence (MVD p. 174). These connections join happiness as human dharma, definite values in relationships, and understanding fulfilled in conduct. Evaluation is the human way of knowingly recognising and fulfilling those relations (§6.1). Statutory law is an institutional codification; its adequacy is judged by whether it supports justice and mutual satisfaction.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Human families and social assemblies achieve continuity through relationship-fulfilment. Their members remain distinct units who recognise relationships, fulfil values, evaluate the fulfilment, and achieve mutual satisfaction. This is the basis of humane continuity in family, community, and society. It gives social assembly a different basis from the definite composition of a chemical compound (§1.5).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Regulation from saturation through order-specific conformance to human justice and participation in universal orderliness

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.14 Realisation in coexistence

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Through realisation, jeevan understands nature as inseparably present in Omnipresence. It knows existence as coexistence, knows itself as the knower, and expresses that understanding as authenticity. This is the goal of development: an activity of jeevan, with the distinction between the knowing unit and the pervasive reality preserved.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Knowledge, knower, and known remain distinguishable in realisation. Jeevan is the knower. The threefold content of knowledge comprises the holistic view of coexistence, knowledge of jeevan, and knowledge of humane conduct. Existence as coexistence is what is seen and known, while the human and jeevan goals become meaningful through awakened participation in undivided society and universal orderliness. Their coherence lies in accurate knowing and evidence, not in ontological identity.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Knowledge (gyan) is also a name for the actionless pervasive reality in which knowing occurs (MVD p. 35). This usage and knowledge as understood content are related through realisation: jeevan knows coexistence without becoming the pervasive reality. Wisdom (vivek) recognises the human goals of resolution, prosperity, fearlessness, and coexistence; science (vigyan) determines how material means and human activity serve those goals (MVD p. 170). Knowing, judging purpose, and arranging its material fulfilment are thus connected but distinguishable.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Realisation settles the search arising from delusion. Ultimate bliss is named at realised atma, and bliss names the harmony of buddhi and atma (§1.9). Authenticity is the projection of realisation: understanding becomes evident through behaviour, work, and participation. Recognition and fulfilment in orderliness are therefore expressions of realisation, not substitutes for it.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: In awakened human living, presentation, communication, and expression carry realised understanding into a shared tradition (AVD pp. 115–116). Presentation (prakashan) makes actuality evident through an accomplished and meaningful form; communication (sampreshana) indicates completeness, including constitutional, activity, and conduct completeness; and expression (abhivyakti) is the mental, verbal, and bodily activity through which one’s existence is evidenced for all-round resolution (abhyudaya) (PS pp. 22, 119, 206). Understanding is thus presented, made understandable, and lived. These activities involve the coherent participation of jeevan through the body described in §1.8. Words direct attention to the activity of units and its inherent meaning, which concerns their properties, essential nature, and dharma; their usefulness is fulfilled in understanding and enabling another to understand (MVD pp. 109–110).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: As a skilful expressive activity, art (kala) makes the qualities of presentation, communication, and expression evident and meaningful, joining usefulness with beauty (PS p. 56). It concerns how understanding and purpose take an accomplished form in speech, work, and behaviour. In making an object, this is evident as the art value that enhances usefulness (§1.13.1); in communicating understanding, it serves intelligibility and the purpose of resolution. The same humane understanding is evidenced through these connected activities.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: A related vocabulary of gross, subtle, causal, and supreme cause identifies different realities: gross forms are compositions and bodies; subtle units are atoms; the causal status is assigned to atma; and Omnipresence is supreme cause (MVD pp. 288–289). These terms do not denote three bodies of a single self as in the Advaita analysis (§2.6).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.15 Ontology and societal fulfilment outcomes

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Human awakening is evidenced through four goals: resolution, prosperity, fearlessness, and coexistence. Resolution is clarity about existence, jeevan, relationships, and conduct, without unresolved contradiction directing action. Prosperity is the family’s assurance of producing more physical goods than its assessed needs and using them appropriately. Fearlessness is trust in human mutuality and society. Coexistence is complementary living among humans and with the rest of nature.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The cumulative correspondence between these goals and the jeevan values is set out in §1.9. Their fulfilment rests on the human aim of continuous happiness, recognition of relationships, and the responsibility to make understanding effective in conduct.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: At the social scale, awakened living develops from family to undivided society and universal orderliness. Five social systems support its continuity. These differ from the four dimensions of individual living—realisation, thought, behaviour, and work—introduced in §1.13.1:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Social system Function in humane orderliness Education–sanskar Makes right understanding and the disposition to live by it available across generations. Justice–preservation Recognises relationships, fulfils values, evaluates fulfilment, achieves mutual satisfaction, and protects humaneness. Health–restraint Maintains a bodily condition and disciplined living capable of supporting and evidencing awakening. Production–work Enables each family to apply labour and skill toward producing more than its assessed physical needs. Exchange–storage Organises exchange through recognition of labour value and maintains responsible reserves for continuity.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: These are not external institutions added to an otherwise private realisation. They are the public structures through which understanding is transmitted, relationships fulfilled, bodies supported, needs met, and social participation sustained.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Humane tradition means continuity across generations. An individual’s conduct completeness contributes to this continuity without depending on the prior awakening of the whole society. Social completeness concerns the wider condition in which resolution, prosperity, fearlessness, and coexistence remain available through education, family, work, and orderliness (MVD pp. 15–16).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.16 Method, evidence, and what Madhyasth Darshan establishes

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan presents its method as study, experiment and practice, followed by realisation and evidence in conduct. These activities do not all warrant the same kind of claim:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Mode of inquiry What it tests or evidences What it does not establish by itself Logical exposition Whether definitions and relations form a coherent account That the premises are empirically true Study and self-examination Whether coexistence, jeevan, and the activities of knowing can be understood and recognised A public physical identification of jeevan Experiment and practice in work and behaviour Whether the proposed understanding regulates action and produces repeatable relational consequences A measurement of constitutional completeness Realisation MD’s claimed first-person completion of knowing coexistence, jeevan, and humane conduct Agreement from methods that do not accept realisation as warrant Conduct-evidence Whether values, mutual satisfaction, resolution, and participation become intersubjectively visible That every ontological claim has thereby become a scientific measurement

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Instrument-based scientific confirmation remains a further comparison standard where a claim concerns publicly detectable physical structure. The current primary-text account supplies no accepted measurement procedure for constitutional completeness, the jeevan–body interface, or post-death reassociation (§6.2).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Living proof (pramanikta) is MD’s practical evidence of understanding: what is understood must guide action and fulfilment in relationships. The comparison that follows distinguishes this standard from the warrants offered by other philosophies and by public scientific measurement.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: 2. The Advaita Vedanta Answer

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Advaita Vedanta holds that existence in the strictest, absolute sense is Brahman alone — one without a second (ekam eva advitiyam). The world of names, forms, bodies, and relations is mithya: a dependent appearance valid at the empirical level (vyavahara), whose claim to independent reality is sublated by knowledge of absolute reality (paramartha). The true Self (Atman) is neither born nor destroyed, because it is ultimately identical with this non-dual Brahman.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: The account here is Shankara-centred classical Advaita. Its principal authorities are the Upanishads, the Brahma Sutra Bhashya, and the Bhagavad Gita Bhashya. Later systematic vocabulary and pedagogical works such as the Vivekachudamani and Drig-Drishya-Viveka are used where they clarify the tradition, but they do not by themselves determine claims disputed within post-Shankara Advaita.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: 2.1 Brahman and absolute existence

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: The Chandogya Upanishad states Advaita’s foundational claim directly:

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: “In the beginning this was Existence alone, One only, without a second.” - CU 6.2.1

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Shankara reads this existence as partless, all-pervasive consciousness, without internal distinction (CU 6.2.1, commentary). The next verse rejects the claim that existence could arise from non-existence (CU 6.2.2). The claim is about the dependence of all name-form on one reality, rather than a temporal event in which non-being becomes being.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: At paramartha, only this one partless reality exists absolutely. Classical Advaita names that absolute as nirguna Brahman — without attributes, actionless, and not an object among objects. Saguna Brahman is the same reality associated with Maya and spoken of as Ishvara: operative at vyavahara, not a second absolute beside the attribute-free ground (§2.6). Paramatman (the Supreme Self) is likewise not a second absolute beside Brahman. When superimposition is removed, the Ishvara–jiva distinction is resolved as a standpoint-dependent distinction rather than two independently existing beings being destroyed (VC, v. 244; §2.6).

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: How that one reality is characterised as Sat-Chit-Ananda and known as turiya follows in §§2.2–2.3; the tiered architecture through which the world appears relative to it is stated in §§2.4–2.5.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: 2.2 Brahman as Sat-Chit-Ananda

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Advaita reads Brahman as sat, chit, and ananda — being, consciousness, and bliss — three expressions indicating the same non-dual reality. The Taittiriya Upanishad provides a central basis for this understanding:

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: “Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite.” - TU 2.1.1

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Shankara treats each word as a separate predicate of that one Brahman — satyam brahma, jnanam brahma, anantam brahma. Truth (satyam) marks what does not change the nature ascertained as its own, and so distinguishes Brahman from mutable things. Knowledge (jnanam) is consciousness itself, Brahman’s nature rather than an activity that changes its agent. Infinity (anantam) is freedom from limitation by time, space, or object (TU 2.1.1, commentary).

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: The bliss sheath in TU 2.5 remains a covering to be discriminated from the Self. A stronger basis for identifying Brahman with bliss is TU 2.7: Brahman is rasa, the essence or fullness through whose attainment one becomes blissful. Advaita therefore uses ananda for limitless completeness rather than a passing affect. Experiential pleasure is not the final referent of the teaching.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: 2.3 Brahman as turiya

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: The Mandukya Upanishad (MU, vv. 3–7) analyses the Self in four quarters. Waking (jagrat) concerns outward experience of gross objects; dream (svapna) concerns inward experience of subtle objects; deep sleep (sushupti) lacks differentiated objects and desires and is described as undifferentiated consciousness abounding in bliss (MU, vv. 3–5). This supplies a first-person route for distinguishing changing experience from the Self. The text also has a cosmic dimension: verse 6 calls the third quarter the Lord of all and the source into which beings resolve. Its quarters are therefore not merely psychological descriptions, but neither are they MD’s developmental orders of nature.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Turiya — the fourth — is not another state alongside these three, but the Self known by negating every state-characteristic:

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: “They consider the Fourth to be that which is not conscious of the internal world, nor conscious of the external world, nor conscious of both the worlds, nor a mass of consciousness, nor conscious, nor unconscious; which is unseen, beyond empirical dealings, beyond the grasp (of the organs of action), uninferable, unthinkable, indescribable; whose valid proof consists in the single belief in the Self; in which all phenomena cease; and which is unchanging, auspicious, and non-dual. That is the Self, and That is to be known.” - MU, v. 7

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Seer-seen discrimination in the Drig-Drishya-Viveka and the Gita’s field-knower teaching develop the same structural point (§2.7).

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: 2.4 Three tiers of reality

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Advaita’s standard framework separates three levels of reality. Apparent errors (pratibhasika) include a rope mistaken for a snake. Shared empirical reality (vyavahara) governs bodies, physical laws, ethics, and scripture. Absolute truth (paramartha) is Brahman alone. Discrimination (viveka) between the real and the unreal is defined as the firm conviction that Brahman alone is real and the universe unreal (VC, v. 20); at the deepest level the individual soul is itself, directly, the Supreme Brahman, and nothing else (VC, v. 216).

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Mithya names the world’s dependent ontological status; the three tiers distinguish the validity of appearances and the knowledge that corrects them.
