Sublation (badha) removes an attribution of reality: correcting the rope-snake removes the belief that a snake is present; knowing Brahman removes the attribution of independent reality to name-form. Knowledge does not turn a previously independent world into an unreal one. Empirical appearances and conduct can continue after the correction (BS 2.1.14; 4.1.15).

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Level What exists? Status of world / error Apparent (pratibhasika) Rope-snake, dream objects, perceptual errors Sublated by waking or correction Empirical (vyavahara) Bodies, minds, Ishvara, causes, duties, scriptures, science Shared, law-governed; operationally valid; sublated only by brahma-jnana Absolute (paramartha) Brahman alone World is mithya, dependent appearance

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: At vyavahara, the world is not unreal in the way a hallucination is; it is unreal relative to Brahman — like a dream relative to waking. The world is not sheer nothing, nor absolutely real; it is mithya — dependent appearance.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Later Advaita systematises this status through anirvacaniyatva, indefinability as absolutely real or sheer non-being. Shankara already describes name-form as indeterminable as identical with or different from Brahman (BS 1.1.5), and as indeterminable as real or unreal (BS 2.1.14). Later accounts elaborate this into theories of mithyatva and error; they should not all be attributed to Shankara as one finished system. The central distinction allows empirical validity without granting the world independent absolute being (§2.10).

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Advaita Vedanta: three tiers of reality (paramartha, vyavahara, pratibhasika), sublation relations, and Maya and moksha

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: 2.5 Maya, adhyasa, and causal doctrine

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: The multiplicity of the world rests on Brahman through superimposition (adhyasa). Shankara’s opening definition is that superimposition is the cognition of something in that which it is not: the apparent presentation, in the form of memory, of something previously seen in another locus (BS, Adhyasa Bhashya). Subject (vishayi, the conscious I) and object (vishaya, body, senses, and world) are opposed like light and darkness, yet ordinary dealing proceeds from their mutual superimposition: bodily predicates are placed on the Self, and the Self’s consciousness is placed on the body.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: The rope mistaken for a snake illustrates this structure. The rope is the substrate (adhishthana) of the error; it does not become a snake. Similarly, Brahman is the reality on which name-form depends, without acquiring its apparent divisions. Later Advaita commonly analyses Maya through concealment (avarana) and projection (vikshepa), and distinguishes cosmic manifestation under Ishvara from individual misidentification under avidya. Later schools disagree about the precise relation between Maya and avidya and about the locus of ignorance. Their common commitment is that name-form has no independent reality apart from Brahman, while the embodied jiva mistakes the body-mind complex for the Self.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Advaita accepts effect–cause non-difference without adopting Samkhya’s real transformation of prakriti. The Chandogya’s clay teaching states the pattern directly: through knowledge of one lump of clay, all things made of clay are known, since every transformation is a matter of speech and name while clay alone is real (CU 6.1.4). Shankara makes the causal point explicit at BS 2.1.14: an effect has no existence apart from its cause. The Vivekachudamani compresses the same teaching: modifications such as a clay jar are nothing but clay; likewise the universe has no being apart from Brahman (VC, v. 251).

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: At the empirical level, Brahman associated with Maya is taught as Ishvara, the non-different material and efficient cause of name-form (abhinna-nimitta-upadana-karana). Yet Brahman does not undergo real modification: the world has no independent being apart from Brahman, while Brahman remains changeless. Later Advaita calls this vivarta, apparent rather than real transformation, in contrast with parinama. Creation is therefore neither production from nothing nor a real alteration of the absolute. Causal instruction belongs to vyavahara and is itself withdrawn at the highest non-dual standpoint.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: The later error theory anirvacaniya-khyati treats the mistaken snake as neither real nor sheer non-being: it is experienced, yet correction removes the belief in its presence. This illustrates dependent appearance without making the shared empirical world equivalent to a particular perceptual error (§2.4). MD also admits mistaken recognition, but locates delusion (bhram) in the real jeevan, especially in its identification of the body as self. It does not extend the category of dependent appearance to the reality of the world itself.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: 2.6 Ishvara, jiva, and jagat at vyavahara

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Because Advaita distinguishes empirical teaching from absolute non-duality, it uses categories structurally necessary to explain the experienced world even though no second reality remains at the absolute standpoint.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Brahman at paramartha is nirguna — pure, actionless awareness. Ishvara (saguna Brahman) is Brahman associated with Maya and taught as the non-different material and efficient cause (abhinna-nimitta-upadana-karana) of name-form manifestation, not a creator ex nihilo. Ishvara and jiva are not two absolutes alongside Brahman. Their distinction is valid within vyavahara and is resolved, rather than annihilated as two independently existing things, when non-dual identity is known (VC, v. 244).

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Jivatman (jiva) is the individual embodied soul — the true Self (Atman) conditioned by upadhis (limiting adjuncts), appearing as separate until realisation. Reflection (pratibimba) and limitation (avaccheda) are two ways later Advaita explains how the one Self appears many under adjuncts. The empirical person is also analysed in terms of three bodies — gross (sthula), subtle (sukshma), and causal (karana) — and five sheaths (pancha kosha: food, vital, mental, intellect, and bliss). These belong to empirical life without constituting an ultimately separate Self. Their shared vocabulary with Madhyasth Darshan does not make the two ontologies equivalent (§5.7.2).

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: In the pedagogical account of the internal organ (antahkarana), manas considers alternatives, buddhi determines, ahamkara identifies as the embodied agent, and chitta remembers (VC, vv. 93–94). These are mental functions illuminated by the Self, not four independently conscious subjects. The reflected-consciousness account explains their apparent consciousness and agency (VC, vv. 103–104; DDV, vv. 1–7). This differs from MD’s placement of its five faculties within the sentient jeevan unit.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Karma and samsara belong to the empirical order: the conditioned jiva continues across births until liberating knowledge, while the subtle body carries the equipment and impressions for experiencing action-results (BG 2.22; VC, vv. 96–100). Ordinary bodily death therefore does not end empirical individuality. Its continuity across births is compatible with the teaching that no separate self is ultimately real.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Jagat (nama-roopa) is the physical universe of names and forms — operationally valid at vyavahara, ultimately mithya at paramartha. Bodies, minds, causal order, scripture, and science belong to this shared tier until brahma-jnana sublates the apparent separateness of the world from Brahman.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: 2.7 Witness-consciousness and the Self

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: The Drig-Drishya-Viveka (DDV) offers a rigorous seer-seen (drig-drishya) discrimination: whatever can be observed — body, sensations, thoughts — is “seen” and therefore not the seer (DDV, vv. 1–5). What remains is Sakshin, witness-consciousness — irreducible to matter, and Advaita’s primary first-person route for discriminating the Self from body and mind.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: The Gita calls the body the field and its knower the knower of the field. Krishna then asks to be known as the knower in all fields and identifies knowledge of both field and knower as knowledge (BG 13.2–13.3 in the cited edition; conventionally 13.1–13.2).

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: The Self is self-luminous (svaprakasha): its presence does not require a second awareness to reveal it, whereas particular thoughts and perceptions can themselves be known (DDV, vv. 1–5). Witness-language expresses this asymmetry during discrimination; it does not posit an ultimately separate witness confronting independently real objects. At liberation the witness is known as Brahman, without a second. Whether irreducible awareness is finally one non-dual Self or many distinct knowers is the dispute in §§5.3.3, 5.6.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: 2.8 Conservation, origination, and temporality

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Brahman does not begin: it is partless, actionless, and outside temporal becoming (VC, v. 393). At the empirical level, manifestation, maintenance, and dissolution (srishti–sthiti–laya) recur without a first cycle. Shankara explicitly defends beginningless transmigration and creation through the mutual dependence of karma and embodiment, like seed and sprout (BS 2.1.35–36). This cosmology gives the empirical world continuity and causal order without making it an independent absolute.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: At paramartha, even origination is denied. Gaudapada’s doctrine of non-origination (ajati) states that neither birth, bondage, seeking nor liberation is ultimately real (MU, Karika II.32, with Shankara’s commentary). The distinction is between levels of explanation, not between two successive histories of Brahman. Temporal succession belongs to the empirical order; the Self does not become timeless at the end of a process.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: The Mandukya analysis of waking, dream, and deep sleep (§2.3) is a first-person route into how temporal states appear and are witnessed; the witness (turiya) is not another state among them. Fuller comparison of Advaita’s trikaal language with Madhyasth Darshan’s account of kaal as duration of unit-activity is developed in Nature of Time.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: 2.9 Liberation and the knowledge path

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Liberation (moksha) is recognition of the ever-established identity of Atman and Brahman, rather than a merger of two independently real beings. The identity teaching tat tvam asi — “That thou art” — belongs to CU 6.8.7 and is developed in Shankara’s treatment of scriptural identity and the individual Self (BS 1.1.4; 1.4.22). The jiva was never ultimately separate; knowledge removes the contrary understanding.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Liberating knowledge can arise while the body lives (jivanmukti). The body’s subsequent continuation is explained through already-begun karma (prarabdha); when that is exhausted, bodily existence ends, conventionally described as videhamukti. Death does not complete an otherwise incomplete liberating knowledge (BS 1.1.4; 4.1.15). Embodied conduct after knowledge remains meaningful at vyavahara (§2.10).

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Method serves that ontological claim rather than replacing it. Advaita inherits the classical analysis of valid knowledge (pramana): for the supreme truth of non-duality, verbal testimony (shabda) — the revealed word of the Upanishads, processed through reasoning and meditation — is finally competent; perception and inference operate within the subject-object duality to be transcended. The path is classically threefold: hearing (shravana), reasoning (manana), and sustained meditation (nididhyasana), under a qualified teacher. Teaching itself often proceeds by provisional attribution and later withdrawal (adhyaropa–apavada): names and forms are first admitted for instruction, then negated until only the Self remains — the same logic as seer-seen discrimination in the DDV. Full epistemological comparison: The Epistemology of Coexistence §2.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: The Vivekachudamani insists on ethical discipline as prerequisite to knowledge (VC, vv. 17–19). Ethics at vyavahara is developed in §2.10.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: 2.10 Ethics, loka-sangraha, and what realisation evidences

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Advaita’s account of the world as mithya at paramartha does not make ethics dispensable where agency and obligation operate. Before knowledge, discipline, duty, non-attachment, and steadiness prepare the mind for inquiry. The Bhagavad Gita, in Shankara’s commentary, also invokes loka-sangraha — holding the world together: action is undertaken without possessiveness or attachment to results, and the knower may continue to act for the welfare and guidance of others (BG 3.8, 3.20–3.25). After knowledge, such action does not reinstate ultimate agency or separate individuality; embodied life continues under the already-begun momentum of prarabdha until the body falls. Jivanmukti (§2.9) therefore joins non-agency at the highest standpoint with responsible conduct at vyavahara.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: What Advaita recognises at the empirical level must be distinguished from what realisation discloses at paramartha. Some disciplines prepare for knowledge; non-attached action and world-welfare also articulate how the knower can live. Empirical responsibility does not require a restoration of ultimate separate agency.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Domain Valid at vyavahara Status at paramartha Ethics and duty Discipline prepares for knowledge; non-attached action and loka-sangraha express knowledge (VC, vv. 17–19; BG 3.8, 3.20–3.25) No separate agent or obligation remains at paramartha; embodied conduct continues at vyavahara World and nature Law-governed, shared, beginningless cosmology Mithya — dependent appearance Individual self Real as embodied jiva under upadhi Identical with Brahman; separateness dispelled Relationships and society Loka-sangraha, ordained action for world-welfare Not ultimately separate from Brahman Time and change Past, present, future, birth and death operationally valid Sublated when timeless Self is known

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Realisation removes the attribution of independent reality to world and individual; it does not change their ontological status or require the disappearance of empirical conduct. The knower can continue to act for world-welfare without taking separate agency as absolute.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: 2.11 Method, evidence, and what Advaita establishes

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Advaita Vedanta answers the study’s framing questions as follows:

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Question Advaita Vedanta answer Section What is existence? Brahman alone — being, consciousness, bliss, one without a second §§2.1–2.3 What exists? Brahman absolutely; jiva, Ishvara, and jagat real only at vyavahara §§2.4, 2.6 Does it begin? Brahman does not begin; name-form cycles as srishti–sthiti–laya within beginningless vyavahara §2.8 Does the self begin? Jivatman is vyavahara-level conditioning; the true Self was never born and never separate §§2.7, 2.9 Is the world real? Operationally real at vyavahara; mithya — dependent appearance — at paramartha §§2.4–2.5 How do we know? Scripture (shabda), reasoning, and contemplative discrimination — shravana, manana, nididhyasana §2.9

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Advaita presents a non-dual ontology and a disciplined first-person method for discriminating seer from seen. Whether its scriptural and contemplative grounds warrant denying ultimate reality to plurality remains the comparative question in §6.3.

passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: 3. Modern Philosophical Approaches

passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: Contemporary Western philosophy contains no single ontology. Physicalism is influential in analytic philosophy of mind and is continuous with much scientific explanation, but it competes with dualism, panpsychism, neutral monism, hylomorphism, idealism, and process metaphysics. The decisive questions are not captured by a simple matter-versus-mind opposition: what counts as physical, whether experience is reducible or fundamental, what individuates a self, how particulars depend on a ground, and whether value belongs to reality or to human practice. SB frames one central dispute by observing that neither one-way emergence has been directly witnessed:

passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: “In this course, metaphysical thought has held that matter arises from consciousness, whereas materialist thought has maintained that consciousness emerges from matter. Both ideologies have proposed numerous arguments, practices, and experiments in support of their claims. Yet, neither has matter been seen emerging from consciousness, nor consciousness emerging from matter. What is evident is that consciousness and matter are inseparably present.” - SB, p. 48

passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan’s own title — Samadhanatmak Bhautikvad (Resolution Centred Materialism) — reframes rather than abandons material reality. Against dialectical materialism, which treats conflict as historically generative, SB proposes an orderliness-centred account in which nature remains real, saturated in Omnipresence, and intelligible through resolution rather than perpetual opposition (SB, pp. 8, 44). That proposal must therefore be compared not only with reductive materialism but with several rival accounts of ground, matter, experience, individuality, and relation.

passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: The figure below maps the principal physicalist family. The later subsections then place it beside dualist, panpsychist, hylomorphic, monist, pluralist, process, and neutral-ground alternatives. These positions disagree sufficiently that they cannot be combined into a single “modern” answer in §5.

passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: Physicalism: one level of reality built upward by composition; causation under conservation laws; observation and public evidence; unsettled hard problem and cosmological beginning

passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: 3.1 Physicalist ontology: what exists

passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: “I take physicalism to be the view that every real, concrete phenomenon in the universe is…physical.” - Strawson 2006, p. 2

passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: Physicalism holds, at minimum, that concrete reality is wholly physical or wholly constituted by the physical. Type-identity and reductive theories identify mental states with physical states; physicalist versions of functionalism identify mental roles with their physical realisations; non-reductive physicalism allows relatively autonomous psychological descriptions while requiring every instance to be physically realised. Emergentist versions assign higher-level properties to organised physical systems. These positions share dependence on the physical while disagreeing about reduction, explanation, and causal autonomy. Functionalism itself specifies causal or computational roles and need not, without a further premise about their realisation, entail physicalism.

passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: Physicalism, methodological naturalism, and scientific realism must be kept separate. Physicalism is a metaphysical thesis about what concrete reality is. Methodological naturalism is a rule of inquiry that seeks testable explanations without invoking non-natural interventions. Scientific realism is a philosophy of science according to which successful mature theories give at least approximate knowledge of a mind-independent world, including unobservable entities. Instrumentalism and constructive empiricism instead restrict commitment to empirical adequacy. Science can be practised under more than one of these philosophical interpretations.

passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: Causal closure supplies a major argument for physicalism: if every physical event has a sufficient physical cause, a non-physical mind seems either causally idle, systematically overdetermining, or in need of a revised causal account (Kim 2005). Closure is not the definition of every physicalism, and non-physical causation cannot be dismissed merely by repeating energy conservation; the conclusion depends on how physical cause, sufficiency, exclusion, and interaction are specified. It nevertheless places a serious burden on Madhyasth Darshan’s claim that jeevan works through a body: the account must explain what difference jeevan makes while accounting for the success of physical descriptions of bodily causation.

passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: 3.2 The hard problem and the first-person datum

passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: “The really hard problem of consciousness is the problem of experience. When we think and perceive, there is a whir of information-processing, but there is also a subjective aspect.” - Chalmers 1995, p. 3

passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: Nagel characterises conscious experience through what it is like for the experiencing organism (1974, p. 1). The hard problem asks why physical processing should have that subjective character, beyond the established correlations between brain activity and experience. Physicalists differ over whether this is a temporary explanatory gap, a conceptual limitation, or a mistaken demand. The gap alone does not establish an extra-physical bearer. Advaita’s seer-seen discrimination (§2.7) and MD’s account of jeevan (§6.2.1) must each support their further ontological claims.

passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: Property dualism does not split the difference within physicalism; it denies that all properties are physical. It holds that conscious properties are irreducible even when they depend lawfully on physical systems. Substance dualism goes further by positing a distinct mental bearer. Both preserve the first-person datum but inherit an interaction or dependence problem: they must explain why conscious properties arise where they do and how they participate in physical action. The explanatory gap therefore creates logical space for non-reductive ontology without selecting Madhyasth Darshan’s constitutionally complete jeevan over dualist, panpsychist, emergentist, or neutral-monist alternatives.

passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: 3.3 Families of response: panpsychism, emergence, and illusionism

passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: The hard problem generates several families that cross the boundary between physicalism and its rivals. Strawson’s “real physicalism” argues that experience is itself physical and that the physical cannot be wholly non-experiential:

passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: “Real physicalism, realistic physicalism, entails panpsychism.” - Strawson 2006, p. 12

passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: His argument starts from the reality of experience and rejects its emergence from a wholly non-experiential base (Strawson 2006, pp. 2, 12). “Physicalist” and “panpsychist” therefore need not name mutually exclusive camps.

passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: Panpsychism is a family rather than one doctrine. Constitutive micropsychism treats macro-experience as constituted from experiential micro-realities; panprotopsychism places proto-experiential properties at the base; cosmopsychism begins with a cosmic subject and derives local subjects; Russellian monism treats physics as revealing relational structure while leaving the intrinsic nature of its bearers open (Chalmers 2016). Madhyasth Darshan fits none of these exactly. It neither distributes experience across material particles nor identifies Omnipresence with a cosmic subject; sentience belongs only to constitutionally complete jeevan (§1.7.1).

passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: Constitutive panpsychism faces the combination problem: facts about many micro-subjects do not transparently entail one unified macro-subject. Cosmopsychism reverses the direction but must then explain decombination or the individuation of local subjects. Integrated information theory supplies a different structural proposal about the unity and boundaries of experience; it does not by itself solve the metaphysical subject-combination problem (§4.6). Madhyasth Darshan avoids micro-subject combination by identifying jeevan as one constitutionally complete unit, but must show how that unit and its claimed sentience can be independently identified (§6.2.1).

passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: Emergentism offers a middle path: new properties appear at organisational thresholds — digestion from chemistry, life from biochemistry, mind from neural complexity. Weak emergence treats higher-level patterns as real but dependent on lower-level physics; strong emergence would add causally novel properties irreducible to microphysics. Constitutional completeness also marks a qualitative threshold, but the resemblance is formal rather than explanatory. Madhyasth Darshan places the transition in a particular atom whose constitution becomes closed and free from molecular and weight bondage; biological emergentism places sentience in organised living systems. The critical question is whether these different proposed thresholds can be operationally distinguished (§6.2.1).

passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: Illusionism instead challenges the conception of phenomenal properties that generates the hard problem. It retains access, self-report, discrimination, and functional control while explaining why experience seems to have properties that the theory denies (Frankish 2016, pp. 1, 8). Eliminative materialism makes a different claim: some folk-psychological categories, especially belief and desire as commonsense theory describes them, may fail to refer and may be replaced by neuroscience (Churchland 1986). Dennett’s functional and heterophenomenological approach belongs near illusionism but should not be treated as identical with Churchland’s eliminativism. These views require MD to clarify the content and reliability of introspection before using it to establish a distinct sentient bearer.

passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: 3.4 The self: personal identity and persistence

passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: The philosophy of personal identity distinguishes the bearer of experience from the criteria by which a person persists. Physicalists usually hold that persons begin and end with some biological or psychologically organised physical system, but they disagree about which continuity matters. Animalism identifies the human person with the living human organism. Psychological-continuity theories privilege memory, intention, character, and connected consciousness. Constitution views distinguish the person from, while materially constituting the person through, the organism. Narrative and embodied-enactive accounts emphasise temporally extended self-interpretation, agency, and bodily engagement.

passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: Parfit argues that what matters in survival may be psychological connectedness and continuity rather than a further, all-or-nothing fact of identity (Parfit 1984; SEP Personal Identity). Animalists object that psychological criteria can come apart from the persistence of the organism; narrative and constitution accounts object that a person is neither a bare organism nor a detachable stream of memories. None of these theories by itself establishes post-death survival, but their disagreements prevent “the self is a brain model” from standing as the single modern philosophical answer.

passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: Substance and simple-subject views preserve a bearer not reducible to psychological continuity: Aquinas’s rational soul is the form of the living body (§3.6.1), while Leibniz’s monads are simple individual substances (§3.6.3). Self-model and predictive-processing accounts in cognitive science explain how bodily ownership, perspective, and continuity are represented without positing an immortal unit (§4.5). The comparison with jeevan must therefore distinguish at least three questions: what produces the experienced sense of self, what makes a person persist, and whether there is an enduring sentient bearer beyond the body.

passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: 3.5 Origination, conservation, and world realism

passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: Western philosophy asks whether what exists had a beginning and whether particulars endure through change. Mainstream physicalism holds that local systems — organisms, stars, civilisations — begin and end, while fundamental physics may or may not require a cosmic beginning (§4.2). Conservation principles in physics treat certain quantities as preserved through transformation — a structural parallel later compared with vastu through roop-change (§1.4, §4.3), though the categories differ.

passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: Scientific realism answers “is the world mind-independent?” affirmatively, while instrumentalism and constructive empiricism restrict commitment to what theories successfully predict or to their observable consequences. Metaphysical idealisms instead take mind, experience, or the conditions of experience as ontologically basic; they cannot be reduced to the claim that objects depend on being presently perceived. Ontological nihilism, mereological nihilism, and moral nihilism answer different questions and should not be combined. Only the first two bear directly on what entities exist; moral nihilism concerns value rather than world-existence.

passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: Philosophy of time adds a further fork. Block-universe eternalism treats past, present, and future as equally real coordinates; presentism privileges the present. Relational theories deny time as an independent container — time is the order of change among things. Cosmological questions about a beginningless substrate are developed in §4.2; the philosophical point here is that Western ontology has no consensus on whether existence as a whole begins, even when particular configurations do. Activity-based accounts of duration are structurally closer to relational and process views than to block eternalism (Nature of Time §3).

passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: Ethics cannot be read directly from physicalism. Evolutionary theory may explain capacities for attachment, cooperation, punishment, and norm learning without deciding whether moral claims are true. Metaethical naturalists identify moral facts with natural facts; non-natural realists treat normativity as irreducible; constructivists ground norms in procedures of practical reason; contractualists appeal to justifiability to others; virtue theories organise ethics around human flourishing; existential approaches treat meaning as achieved through commitment. Adaptation is a biological outcome, not by itself an account of what a person ought to value or of life’s ultimate purpose.

passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: 3.6 Alternative Western ontologies

passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: The following ontologies are not historical curiosities appended to a physicalist consensus. Each remains a distinct answer to the relation between ground and particulars, the individuation and persistence of selves, causation, and teleology. Their comparisons with Madhyasth Darshan are structural rather than claims of identity.

passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: 3.6.1 Hylomorphism and soul-as-form

passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: Aristotelian hylomorphism understands a living substance through matter and form: the soul is the principle by which the body is alive, rather than an additional body inside it. Aquinas develops this account by treating the rational soul as both the body’s substantial form and a subsistent principle capable of surviving bodily death. The human person is nevertheless the soul–body composite; a separated soul is not the complete human being (Aquinas, ST I, q. 75, aa. 2, 4, 6; q. 76, a. 1). This further account of subsistence should not be attributed without qualification to every Aristotelian position.

passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: The comparison with Madhyasth Darshan concerns substantial unity. For Aquinas, soul and matter constitute one human substance. MD’s joint form joins a constitutionally complete sentient jeevan with a pranic body through which it acts; jeevan is not the body’s substantial form. Both accounts can affirm many enduring souls or selves. The difference lies in what each bearer is and how embodiment belongs to it, not in whether there is one conscious bearer per body (§§1.7–1.9).

passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: 3.6.2 Spinoza: substance and modes

passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: For Spinoza, God or Nature is one substance with infinitely many attributes; thought and extension are the attributes considered in his account of mind and body. Particular things are modes of this substance, not independent substances or parts that assemble it (Ethics, I, Def. 6, Props. 14–15). His parallelism relates the order of ideas to the order of things (II, Prop. 7). MD instead affirms units saturated in satta, without treating them as its modifications, and locates active sentience only in jeevan. Spinoza also rejects final causes in nature (I, Appendix), whereas MD makes completeness and fulfilled participation central to its account of activity. These are differences of dependence, consciousness, and purpose, despite the shared refusal of an external maker standing outside nature.

passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: 3.6.3 Leibniz: monads and harmony

passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: Leibniz’s monads are simple, partless substances. Each represents multiplicity through perception, which he distinguishes from reflective awareness. They cannot naturally arise or perish through composition or decomposition, although they depend on God for their existence (Monadology, §§1–7, 14–19). Plurality and persistence permit a comparison with jeevan, but the constitutional difference is decisive: a monad has no parts, while MD describes jeevan through a nucleus and orbital faculties. Perception also belongs to monads generally, whereas MD distinguishes insentient material units from sentient jeevan.

passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: Monads are windowless: their coordination rests on pre-established harmony rather than efficient interaction between created substances (Monadology, §§7, 78–81). MD instead describes jeevan operating through a body in real mutuality. Its orderliness belongs to coexistence rather than to a creator’s harmonisation of independently unfolding monadic histories.

passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: 3.6.4 Process philosophy: occasions and becoming

passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: Whitehead’s process philosophy shares relational realism and refusal of nature bifurcation. His basic units are “actual entities” — “drops of experience, complex and interdependent” (Whitehead 1929, p. 28). The ultimate for Whitehead is creativity, the principle by which the many prior occasions become one new occasion; each occasion’s concrescence — its growing-together from that inherited data — aims at intensity of experience before it perishes (Whitehead 1929). The key contrast remains persistence: Whitehead’s occasions are momentary and “perpetually perish” subjectively, gaining “objective immortality” only as data for successors (Whitehead 1929, p. 44), whereas Madhyasth Darshan’s jeevan is a persisting immortal individual. Process metaphysics also treats time as internal to becoming — a partial affinity with activity-based kaal (§3.5; Nature of Time §3.3).

passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: “Actual entities ‘perpetually perish’ subjectively, but are immortal objectively.” - Whitehead 1929, p. 44

passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: 3.6.5 Neutral monism: common ground

passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: Russell proposes analysing mind and matter through constituents that, considered in isolation, are neither mental nor material (The Analysis of Mind, Lecture I, printed p. 25). Mach likewise treats the psychical and physical as different connections among common elements rather than two kinds of substance (The Analysis of Sensations, Ch. XIV, printed p. 310). These approaches challenge the initial mind–matter division; they do not simply add a third substance beneath two unchanged domains.

passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: The resemblance to MD is limited to refusing to classify the ground as an ordinary mind or material object. Neutral constituents enter the analysis of mind and matter, whereas satta does not transform into units or constitute them as its parts. Units remain real and active while the ground remains actionless.

passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: 3.6.6 Berkeley: spirits and ideas

passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: Berkeley’s idealism distinguishes active spirits from passive ideas. Sensible objects are collections of ideas dependent on perception; their order and involuntary character distinguish the experienced world from private imagination. Divine agency accounts for that order (Principles of Human Knowledge, §§2–3, 25–33, 89). MD also recognises active knowers, but affirms insentient units whose existence does not depend on being perceived. Berkeley retains plural spirits and God, so his idealism is not Advaita’s ultimate non-duality either. This is one representative idealism, not a definition of every idealist philosophy.

passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: These alternatives disagree about dependence, embodiment, relation, and persistence. Hylomorphic substances, Spinozist modes, Leibnizian monads, process occasions, neutral constituents, and Berkeleyan spirits cannot be treated as interchangeable names for MD’s units.

passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: 3.7 Method, evidence, and what philosophy establishes

passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: Modern Western philosophy yields several rival answers rather than one typical ontology. The following families group explanatory strategies and can overlap; Strawson’s physicalist panpsychism is one example. The final column summarises the named alternatives individually, not as a shared doctrine:

passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: Question Physicalist family Panpsychist / neutral-monist family Other alternatives What is fundamental? Physical entities, structures, events, or processes Experience, proto-experience, or neutral intrinsic reality underlying physical structure Form–matter substances, Spinoza’s substance, monads, process occasions, or spirits and ideas What is consciousness? Identical with, realised by, emergent from, or functionally modelled in physical systems Fundamental or rooted in the intrinsic nature of the physical Power of an organised living substance, or a feature of actual occasions What is the self? Organism, psychological continuity, constituted person, narrative or self-model Unified subject whose derivation remains contested Embodied substance, persisting soul-form, or temporally ordered process Does the individual survive bodily death? passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: The hard problem exposes an explanatory obligation for reductive accounts, but it does not establish which non-reductive alternative is true. Physicalism, dualism, panpsychism, hylomorphism, neutral monism, and process metaphysics distribute the burdens differently: reduction, interaction, combination, individuation, or persistence remains difficult in each. None establishes constitutionally complete jeevan or post-death continuity merely from the existence of experience.

passages.heading: 3-modern-philosophical-approaches
passages.text: Modern science constrains these ontologies through measurement and prediction without, by that success alone, choosing one complete metaphysics. Its findings must therefore be stated separately.

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: 4. Modern Scientific Approaches

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: Modern science seeks publicly testable regularities through observation, instrumentation, mathematical modelling, controlled intervention, replication, and criticism. Its ordinary models do not invoke non-physical intervention, but that methodological practice is not identical with the metaphysical thesis that only the physical exists. Scientific results constrain ontologies; they do not by themselves settle whether scientific realism, instrumentalism, structural realism, physicalism, or a non-reductive metaphysics is finally correct.

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan likewise connects evidence with experimentation, behaviour, and experience, while seeking comprehensive resolution through them (SB, p. 44). It treats the human body as provisioned to express understanding (JV, p. 59). Comparing its evidence standard with science requires distinguishing measured mechanisms from claims about what understands and how understanding becomes evident in living.

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: Modern science concept map: empirical method constrains cosmology and spacetime, fields and conservation, thermodynamics and living organisation, mind and self-models, competing consciousness theories, and ecology without by itself determining a complete metaphysics or ultimate value

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: 4.1 Scientific scope and ontological restraint

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: Physics models spacetime, fields, particles, interactions, and thermodynamic regularities. Biology models living organisation, inheritance, evolution, development, and ecological relation. Neuroscience and cognitive science study the neural and computational conditions associated with perception, action, self-representation, and reportable experience. None of these disciplines requires a complete inventory of everything that can exist before inquiry begins.

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: This restraint cuts in both directions. The success of physical models is evidence that physical structure and causal regularity cannot be ignored; it is not a proof that experience has been reductively explained. Conversely, the hard problem and the first-person datum do not establish an immortal jeevan. A responsible comparison asks what each model predicts, what it leaves open, and what additional claim would be required to move from empirical result to ontology.

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: 4.2 Cosmology, spacetime, and cosmic history

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: The ΛCDM model reconstructs an observable universe developing from an early hot, dense state over roughly 13.8 billion years. Measurements of the cosmic microwave background, large-scale structure, expansion, and light-element abundance strongly support this history under the model. They do not establish creation from absolute non-being or prove that the hot early epoch was the first state of all existence (Planck Collaboration 2020).

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: General relativity treats spacetime geometry as dynamical: matter-energy and geometry constrain one another, while cosmological solutions describe expansion and, under classical extrapolation, singular boundaries. Alternative cosmological proposals explore whether those boundaries indicate a physical beginning or the breakdown of the classical model. Loop quantum cosmology models a bounce from a prior contracting phase (Ashtekar and Singh 2011); conformal cyclic cosmology proposes successive aeons (Penrose 2010); eternal inflation allows continuing inflation beyond an observable bubble (Guth 2007). These programs are mutually different and remain speculative. Their possibility shows only that current cosmology does not settle the metaphysical beginninglessness of existence.

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan treats kaal as duration of unit-activity, numerically reckoned by humans within existence (§1.4; SB, pp. 65, 251; MVD, pp. 34, 195), while satta is timeless because it is non-transforming. Relativity instead incorporates temporal relations within physical geometry. The comparison therefore concerns both ontology and level: measured spacetime is part of the physical model, whereas MD’s kaal is an account of how duration belongs to activity. Fuller comparison appears in Nature of Time.

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: 4.3 Quantum fields, particles, and conservation

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: Quantum field theory represents particles as quantised excitations of fields. Particle–antiparticle annihilation and pair creation are not transitions between being and absolute non-being: field states change while conserved quantities appropriate to the interaction are respected. Particle number itself need not be conserved, and fields are not “conserved entities.” Conservation applies to particular quantities through symmetries and dynamical conditions (Weinberg 1995).

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: This permits a limited structural comparison with Madhyasth Darshan’s claim that vastu persists through changes of roop (§1.4), but the categories remain different. A QFT excitation is not an eternal bounded ikai, and a conservation law does not establish the perpetuity of every entity. In general relativity, global energy conservation is additionally subtle because a generic expanding spacetime lacks the global time-translation symmetry required for a simple conserved total energy (Carroll 2010).

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: Nor is satta a physical field. Dynamical fields carry energy-momentum, interact, and vary; satta is described as formless, actionless, and non-transforming (§1.2). A quantum vacuum is a physical state with field correlations and fluctuations. In some theories, non-zero field expectation values and spontaneous symmetry breaking are important features; boundary-dependent vacuum effects also have observable consequences. These are not universal properties of every field or vacuum. Their physical and theory-specific character prevents identifying a quantum vacuum with actionless Omnipresence (Weinberg 1995).

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: 4.4 Thermodynamics, living organisation, and evolution

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: Thermodynamic entropy is a statistical quantity associated with the multiplicity of microscopic states compatible with a macroscopic description. For an isolated macroscopic system, entropy does not decrease, apart from statistical fluctuations; “disorder” is only a rough metaphor. A subsystem can become more organised while exporting entropy to its surroundings, as organisms and ecosystems do through exchanges of energy and matter. A closed system can still exchange heat, so closedness alone does not require its entropy to increase (Tong, Statistical Physics, §§1.2.1, 4.3.3). MD’s vyavastha concerns orderliness, participation, and appropriate conduct, which thermodynamic entropy neither measures nor directly evaluates.

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: Autopoiesis describes living organisation as a self-producing network that continually regenerates the components and boundary through which the network exists (Maturana and Varela 1980, p. 78). It is a theory of living organisation, not by itself a criterion of consciousness. Its organisational closure resembles self-maintenance but not gathanpurnata: autopoiesis concerns metabolic networks, whereas Madhyasth Darshan identifies constitutional completeness with a particular sentient atom.

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: Evolutionary biology explains common descent and adaptation through heritable variation, selection, drift, recombination, developmental constraint, and ecological inheritance. It reconstructs branching lineages rather than a predetermined linear ascent. Origin-of-life research addresses the transition from non-living chemistry to self-maintaining and evolvable systems and should not be conflated with evolution after replication and heredity exist. Madhyasth Darshan’s niyati-kram instead describes an ordered manifestation of material, pranic, animal, and knowledge orders (§1.6). Relating that ontological ordering to phylogeny, extinction, common descent, and multiple evolutionary lineages remains an open task (§6.2.3).

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: 4.5 Mind, self-models, and the end of measurable function

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: Self-model theories explain minimal selfhood, bodily ownership, perspective, agency, and continuity through representations maintained by an embodied cognitive system (Metzinger 2003; Limanowski and Blankenburg 2013). Predictive-processing and active-inference frameworks model perception and action through hierarchical generative models, precision-weighted prediction errors, and policies that keep an organism within viable bounds (Friston 2010; Clark 2016). Prediction error, surprisal, and variational free energy are related formal quantities, not interchangeable names for one process.

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: These frameworks show how self-related experience may be organised without positing an immortal unit. They do not constitute the only scientific theory of personal identity, and a model of bodily self-representation does not by itself decide whether there is a further bearer of experience. Seth’s “controlled hallucination” formulation emphasises that perceptual experience is an embodied, evidence-constrained construction, not that the world or self is an arbitrary fantasy (Seth 2021).

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: The cited United States consensus guideline treats brain death/death by neurologic criteria as death of the person, assessed through permanent loss of brain function as a whole and specified clinical criteria (AAN/AAP/CNS/SCCM 2023). That determination does not independently prove that no non-physical subject survives. The narrower conclusion relevant here is that accepted measurement has not established post-death continuity of an individual subject, while the capacities through which a person communicates and acts cease when the relevant organismal and neural functions are permanently lost.

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: 4.6 Competing scientific theories of consciousness

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: Consciousness science has no settled explanatory theory. Global neuronal workspace theory associates conscious access with widespread availability produced by recurrent amplification and global broadcasting (Dehaene and Changeux 2011). Higher-order theories require an appropriate representation of a mental state as one’s own (Lau and Rosenthal 2011). Recurrent-processing theory locates a sufficient condition in recurrent sensory processing without always requiring global broadcast (Lamme 2006). These theories primarily target access, report, metacognition, or perceptual awareness and make different neural predictions.

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: Integrated Information Theory 4.0 begins from proposed phenomenal properties — intrinsicality, information, integration, exclusion, and composition — and seeks their physical counterparts in a system’s irreducible cause–effect structure (Albantakis et al. 2023). It is not adequately described as a single numerical Φ threshold that produces a self. Its exclusion principle and maximal complexes propose boundaries for experience, but the theory does not establish immortal individuality or solve the philosophical combination problem simply by quantifying integration.

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: The 2025 adversarial collaboration between IIT and global neuronal workspace theory tested preregistered predictions using fMRI, MEG, and intracranial recordings. The results challenged important predictions of both programs and did not select a settled winner (COGITATE Consortium 2025). The scientifically important contrast with Madhyasth Darshan is methodological: these programs expose system-level criteria to measurement, while the primary MD texts identify a constitutionally complete sentient atom without supplying a corresponding physical detection procedure (§6.2.1).

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: 4.7 Ecology, cooperation, and the limits of biological function

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: Ecology treats organisms as participants in networks of energy flow, nutrient cycling, predation, competition, symbiosis, and niche construction. Nowak’s five mechanisms for the evolution of cooperation are kin selection, direct reciprocity, indirect reciprocity, network reciprocity, and group selection (2006). Such models explain conditions under which cooperation can arise or persist; they do not establish that moral obligation is merely reproductive advantage.

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan makes a different claim. It treats complementarity, essentiality-as-value, and definite relationships as structures of coexistence, and it assigns value-recognition and fulfilment distinctively to the knowledge order (§1.13.1). At the human–nature relation it names utility (upyogita) and art (kala) — making natural abundance usable and enhancing that usefulness through skilled and aesthetic labour (MVD pp. 56–57, 324; JV p. 77). Biological function, ecological dependence, and coexistential value may overlap in cases, but they answer different questions.

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: Adaptation and survival are therefore not science’s answer to life’s ultimate purpose. They are explanatory outcomes within evolutionary models. Questions of flourishing, obligation, meaning, and final ends belong to philosophical and practical reasoning informed, but not settled, by biology.

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: 4.8 Method, evidence, and what science establishes

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: Question Empirical scientific position Metaphysical issue left open What physical structures are observed? Dynamical spacetime, quantum fields and excitations, organisms, brains, and ecological systems Whether physical structure exhausts existence Did existence begin? ΛCDM describes an early hot dense epoch and subsequent observable history Whether that epoch is an absolute beginning What happens to the measurable person at death? Integrated organismal and neural capacities irreversibly cease under accepted death criteria Whether any non-physical bearer survives What explains self-experience? Competing models of embodiment, prediction, access, recurrence, integration, and metacognition Whether those models explain phenomenal subjectivity completely What explains cooperation? Evolutionary, ecological, developmental, and cultural mechanisms Whether value and obligation reduce to those mechanisms How are claims tested? Observation, instrumentation, modelling, intervention, replication, and peer criticism Whether first-person or conduct evidence warrants additional ontology

passages.heading: 4-modern-scientific-approaches
passages.text: Science has established powerful mechanisms, quantitative constraints, and corrigible histories. It has not established immortal jeevan, constitutional completeness at gathanpurnata, or post-death continuity. Equally, its methodological success does not by itself prove metaphysical physicalism. The comparison in §5 must preserve both limits.

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: 5. Comparison

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan, Advaita Vedanta, contemporary metaphysics, and modern science do not all offer the same kind of theory. The first two are comprehensive darshanas joining ontology, epistemology, liberation, and conduct. Contemporary philosophy contains rival metaphysical families. Science supplies empirically constrained models that admit more than one philosophical interpretation. Comparison is valid only when these differences of level are kept explicit.

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: The comparison therefore begins with common criteria rather than alliances. It asks what each view takes as fundamental, how it individuates beings, how particulars depend on a ground, what persists through change, what consciousness and selfhood are, how claims are justified, and whether value or purpose belongs to reality. Limited pairwise agreements emerge only after those axes are clear.

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: 5.1 Criteria for comparison

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: Ten criteria organise the comparison:

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: Ontological primitives: what is taken as fundamental.

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: One–many structure and individuation: what makes an individual distinct.

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: Dependence between ground and particulars.

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: The world’s status and persistence.

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: Causation and transformation.

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: Consciousness, selfhood, and survival.

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: Time and cosmic history.

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: Method and evidence.

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: Value, ethics, and purpose.

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: Exposure to empirical or experiential correction.

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: These axes reveal limited agreements without implying shared foundations. Madhyasth Darshan and Advaita both oppose reductive accounts of the first person, but panpsychism, dualism, and hylomorphism also do so. Madhyasth Darshan and scientific realism affirm a mind-independent world, but science does not establish MD’s stronger claim that the world and all units are perpetual. Advaita and standard scientific accounts both decline to establish an eternal distinct individual self, but Advaita reaches that result through non-dual shabda and realisation, while science reports the dependence of measurable personal capacities on living organisation.

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: Ten criteria for comparing Madhyasth Darshan, Advaita Vedanta, contemporary metaphysics, and modern science without conflating philosophical and empirical levels

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: Comparative clarity thus depends on naming both the question and the kind of answer being offered: metaphysical commitment, empirical model, contemplative disclosure, or criterion of conduct.

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: 5.2 Cross-tradition summary

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: The first table compares metaphysical positions. “Physicalism” groups positions united by physical dependence. Panpsychist and neutral-monist strategies receive a separate column to make their claims about intrinsic nature visible; the headings can overlap, as Strawson’s physicalist panpsychism shows (§3.3).

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: Question Madhyasth Darshan Advaita Vedanta Physicalist family Panpsychist / neutral-monist family What is fundamental? Coexistence of Omnipresence and real units Brahman alone at paramartha Physical entities, structures, events, or processes Experience, proto-experience, or neutral intrinsic nature with physical structure What individuates a self? One constitutionally complete jeevan, permanently distinct Individuality belongs to conditioned jiva; true Self is non-dual Brahman Organism, psychological continuity, constitution, narrative, or cognitive organisation Unified subject; derivation from micro- or cosmic reality remains contested Does the individual survive bodily death? Yes; jeevan is immortal Empirical jiva continues through rebirth until liberation; ultimately the Self was never separate Generally no on standard accounts Not entailed by fundamental experience alone What is the world’s status?
