Transforming units in actionless satta through shram–gati–parinam Empirical effect–cause non-difference and vivarta; causal teaching withdrawn at paramartha Dynamical dependence, mechanism, emergence, laws, and constraints Constitution, combination, grounding, or neutral realisation What is time? Duration of unit-activity; satta timeless Time valid at vyavahara, absent from non-dual Brahman Eternalism, presentism, relational and process accounts compete Varies by theory

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: Their epistemic and axiological commitments complete the metaphysical comparison:

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: Question Madhyasth Darshan Advaita Vedanta Physicalist family Panpsychist / neutral-monist family How is the view known? Study, experiment and practice, realisation, conduct-evidence Shabda, reasoning, contemplative discrimination Argument plus continuity with public science Argument from experience and limits of structural explanation Where does value enter? Values and relationships are structurally real; humane conduct evidences awakening Dharma and non-attached action at vyavahara; liberation through knowledge Metaethical positions range from realism to constructivism; physicalism alone does not decide Not fixed by the ontology of consciousness

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: Empirical science supplies the constraints summarised in §4.8: publicly testable models of physical history, living organisation, and cognition. It does not occupy another column as a single complete metaphysics. Its findings matter across these positions, especially where they make claims about bodily function, causal interaction, and survival.

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: 5.3 Key contrasts

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: 5.3.1 Ground and existence

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: Existence itself is answered differently at the root. Madhyasth Darshan holds eternally present coexistence (saha-astitva): formless Omnipresence (satta) and countless real units (ikai) held in saturation, neither made from the other (§1.2). Advaita holds Brahman alone — being, consciousness, and limitless fullness without a second — as absolutely real; the manifold world has no independent being at the highest truth (§2.4). Physicalism takes concrete physical reality as exhaustive, though its members disagree about reduction and emergence (§3.1). Panpsychism and Russellian or neutral monism question whether physics reveals the intrinsic nature of that reality (§3.3, §3.6.5). Hylomorphism, Spinoza, Leibniz, and Whitehead supply further schemes of form–matter substance, modes of one substance, plural monads, and relational occasions (§3.6). None reproduces MD’s two-term coexistence of actionless satta and permanently distinct units.

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: 5.3.2 World realism

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: Whether the world retains final ontological weight divides Madhyasth Darshan from Advaita. Madhyasth Darshan holds jagat satat: the world remains real alongside the changeless ground (MVD, p. 13; §1.4). Advaita makes the empirical world robust for knowledge, duty, and liberation while denying it independent absolute being (§§2.4–2.5). Scientific realism agrees with MD only on mind-independence and investigability; it does not establish that the world or every unit is perpetual. Instrumentalism and constructive empiricism withhold even the realist inference from predictive success. The valid alignment is therefore MD with scientific realism against final world-subordination, not MD with science as such against Advaita.

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: 5.3.3 Self, consciousness, and survival

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan holds many immortal, constitutionally complete jeevan units that work through bodies (§§1.7–1.8). Advaita holds that the true Self is Brahman and that separate jivatman belongs to conditioning at vyavahara (§2.6). Reductive and functional physicalisms identify selfhood with an organism, psychological organisation, or representational process; animalism, constitution, narrative, and enactive accounts supply different criteria of persistence (§3.4). Panpsychism makes experience fundamental but does not thereby secure an immortal personal subject, while hylomorphism and Leibniz preserve stronger individual bearers (§3.6). Scientific self-models explain bodily ownership, perspective, and regulation, and accepted death criteria mark the irreversible end of measurable personal function; neither result alone settles the metaphysical bearer question (§4.5).

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: 5.3.4 Causation and beginninglessness

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: The positions diverge over whether effects have being apart from causes, whether a ground transforms, what individuates a persisting entity, and whether causal discourse is fundamental. Advaita teaches effect–cause non-difference and apparent transformation at vyavahara while withdrawing causal plurality at paramartha. Madhyasth Darshan separates non-transforming mahakaran from transforming units. Physical theories use dynamics, symmetries, constraints, probabilities, and boundary conditions rather than one universal doctrine of efficient causation. Emergentist, process, and hylomorphic accounts add distinct dependence relations. §5.4 compares these without treating conservation laws as metaphysical causes.

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: 5.3.5 Method and what counts as evidence

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: The traditions use different but overlapping criteria for knowing. Madhyasth Darshan joins study through observation, examination, and survey (MVD pp. 88, 115), experiment and practice in behaviour and work (MVD p. 88; SB p. 44), and anubhav whose understanding becomes evident in humane conduct and tradition (MVD pp. 12, 88). Advaita treats Upanishadic shabda as uniquely competent for non-dual Brahman, with reasoning and contemplative discrimination removing contrary understanding (§2.9). Philosophy tests coherence, explanatory power, entailment, and fit with experience and science. Science tests operational predictions through observation, modelling, intervention, replication, and public criticism (§4.1).

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: Inquiry Principal method Claimed reach Exposed limitation Madhyasth Darshan Study → experiment and practice → realisation → conduct-evidence Coexistence, jeevan, and humane order Needs clearer intersubjective criteria for constitutionally complete jeevan Advaita Shabda, reasoning, contemplative discrimination Non-dual identity and removal of superimposition Its authority and sublation criterion are not shared by rival traditions Contemporary philosophy Conceptual argument, phenomenology, explanatory comparison, continuity with knowledge Coherence and comparative plausibility of ontologies Persistent disagreement and limited decisive tests Modern science Observation, instrumentation, modelling, intervention, replication Public mechanisms, regularities, histories, and constraints Does not alone decide a complete metaphysics or ultimate value

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: No single tribunal settles every claim, but the views are not beyond comparison. Each can be tested for internal consistency, fidelity to its sources, phenomenological adequacy, fit with established public knowledge, clarity about what would count against it, and whether its practical evidence follows from its ontology. Fuller epistemology appears in The Epistemology of Coexistence §1.6 and §5.3.

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: 5.3.6 Ethics and life’s purpose

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan makes value and relationship structural to coexistence and treats awakened humane conduct (manaviya aacharan) as evidence of understanding (§§1.13.1, 1.15). Advaita seeks moksha through knowledge of identity with Brahman; discipline prepares for knowledge, while non-attached action and loka-sangraha express knowledge without restoring ultimate agency (§2.10). Physicalism alone decides no ethics. Naturalist realism, non-natural realism, constructivism, contractualism, virtue ethics, and existential accounts remain open within broadly naturalistic philosophy (§3.5). Evolution and ecology explain capacities, functions, and consequences; adaptation and survival are not normative conclusions or ultimate purposes (§4.7). The comparison must therefore keep biological function, moral justification, liberation, and coexistential fulfilment distinct.

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: 5.4 Causal doctrine: effect–cause non-difference, Vivartavada, and transformation

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: Causal doctrine exposes how differently the views understand dependence, transformation, persistence, and explanation (§5.3.4).

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: Advaita: the Chandogya clay teaching and Shankara’s commentary on BS 2.1.14 establish effect–cause non-difference: the effect has no being apart from the cause. At vyavahara, Brahman associated with Maya is taught as both intelligent and material cause, while name-form appears without real alteration of Brahman. Later Advaita calls this vivarta in contrast with parinama. At paramartha, cause, effect, Ishvara, and world are not independent second realities, so causal teaching is ultimately withdrawn rather than promoted into a final mechanism.

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan: Satta is mahakaran, the non-transforming sustaining condition rather than an efficient maker (§1.4). It is neither efficient cause (nimitta) — it performs no action and issues no commands — nor material cause (upadana) that becomes the units. Units of nature undergo real transformation through shram–gati–parinam; compositions form and decompose, while vastu persists through changes of roop. Development, constitutional completeness, awakening, order-specific cycles, and sanskar-mediated human continuity cannot be reduced to one linear chain. The resemblance to parinamavada is limited to real transformation at the level of units; MD rejects the thesis that one material cause transforms into the entire plurality.

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: Classical Samkhya affirms two kinds of irreducible principle: many conscious witnesses (purusha) and one active, non-conscious prakriti. Its twenty-four-principle material account includes root prakriti and twenty-three evolutes; purusha is distinct from that sequence (Samkhya Karika 3, 18–22). Intellect (buddhi) and mind (manas) belong to non-conscious prakriti (Karikas 22, 27), whereas MD places its five faculties within sentient jeevan. The resemblance in plural conscious bearers therefore has a limit: Samkhya’s purusha is an inactive witness, while MD’s jeevan is active. Samkhya’s liberation is discriminative disengagement (kaivalya, Karikas 62–68); MD’s awakening fulfils participation in coexistence. These different final aims do not by themselves establish how responsibly adherents of either view live.

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: Physical explanation and its metaphysical interpretation must be distinguished. Physics uses dynamical equations, symmetries, conserved quantities, probabilistic transitions, spacetime structure, constraints, and boundary conditions. These are not all instances of classical efficient causation, and conservation laws are not themselves causes. Biological explanation adds mechanism, development, function, selection, and historical dependence. A physicalist interpretation denies the need for a non-physical sustaining ground, while emergentist and process views disagree about whether higher-level causation or internal becoming is irreducible.

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: Aspect Advaita Madhyasth Darshan Physical explanation Process / emergent alternatives Ground–effect relation Effect has no being apart from Brahman at vyavahara Units coexist in satta but are not made from it Models systems through physical structure and history; no transcendent ground appears in the model Becoming or higher-level organisation may be irreducible Does the ground transform? Brahman does not; vivarta names apparent transformation Satta does not; units really transform Fields and spacetime can be dynamical; no universal static substrate is established Whitehead’s creativity is expressed through perishing occasions; strong emergence posits novel powers What persists? Brahman; name-form lacks independent being Real units and vastu through roop-change Theory-specific conserved quantities and causal/structural continuities Organised substance, processual inheritance, or emergent pattern Does causation remain ultimate? No; causal plurality is withdrawn at paramartha Real unit-activity remains within perpetual coexistence Usually yes as physical dependence or dynamics, though its interpretation varies Relation, form, process, or emergence may be more basic than efficient cause Beginninglessness Brahman beginningless; empirical cycles taught within vyavahara Coexistence and units do not arise from abhava Observable cosmic history is finite under ΛCDM; absolute beginning unsettled Varies by system

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: The comparison shows why conservation cannot be used as a direct scientific confirmation of either vivarta or MD’s perpetual units. It supports transformation without creation from everyday nothing in specific models; the ontological interpretation remains additional.

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: 5.5 Entity comparison

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: The overview in §5.2 does not make similarly positioned concepts equivalent. This section identifies the principal mismatches between proposed counterparts, then distinguishes an entity’s constitution from its relations and scientific description. Abrahamic and Dvaita ontologies remain outside scope.

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: MD concept Proposed counterpart Why the concepts are not interchangeable Ground: satta Brahman, Spinoza’s substance, or neutral constituents Brahman alone is ultimately real; Spinoza’s particulars are modes; neutral constituents enter the constitution of mind and matter. MD’s units are neither appearances nor modifications nor parts of satta. Sentient bearer: jeevan Atman, rational soul, monad, or actual occasion Atman is non-dual; Aquinas’s soul is the body’s substantial form; a monad is partless; Whitehead’s occasion perishes subjectively. MD’s sentient atom has a closed constitution and remains individually distinct. Material embodiment: body Advaita’s gross body or a physicalist organism Advaita gives the body empirical reality; physicalist accounts make physical organisation sufficient for concrete embodiment. MD’s body is a real pranic composition operating jointly with jeevan.

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: MD affirms both definite bearers and real relations. Boundary, constitution, capacity, order, and dharma belong to the unit; manifested guna, usefulness, and fulfilled participation become evident in mutuality. A bearer is therefore neither an empty relational position nor something whose contribution can be understood wholly in isolation (§§1.3, 1.13.1).

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: Relational dependence does not have the same meaning in every ontology. Whitehead makes inherited relations constitutive of a new occasion; Aquinas’s formal cause explains the unity of a living substance; Leibniz coordinates monads without efficient interaction. None is simply the saturation relation of units in actionless satta (§§3.6, 5.4). Their accounts of fulfilment also require their own premises. Hylomorphic flourishing, Whiteheadian intensity, Advaita’s liberation, and MD’s humane conduct cannot be inferred merely from the shared word “relation.”

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: Scientific entities are identified within models and procedures: a particle by its physical properties and interactions, an organism by its living organisation, and a neural correlate through measurable relations to experience or behaviour. Equating any of these with an ontological category requires shared identifying criteria. Similar words such as “atom,” “energy,” or “order” do not supply those criteria. Conversely, a metaphysical claim about a unit’s bodily effects remains answerable to relevant observations even when its full interpretation exceeds the scientific model (§§4.3–4.6, 6.2).

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: 5.6 The Sat-Chit-Ananda contrast, distributed

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: Advaita’s Sat-Chit-Ananda and Madhyasth Darshan’s coexistence both speak of being, consciousness, and fulfilment. The contrast concerns what those words name and whether world and individual plurality retain ultimate reality. It develops the ground and sentient-bearer comparison in §5.5.1.

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: For Advaita, sat, chit, ananda are three names for one ultimate reality without a second; the world is finally mithya. For Madhyasth Darshan, the same vocabulary is distributed across coexistence, not compressed into one subject:

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: Concept Advaita Vedanta (Unified Non-Dualism) Madhyasth Darshan (Distributed Coexistence) Sat (Being) Brahman alone is absolutely real; the world’s attributed independent reality is sublated. Beingness (astitva) is coexistence of formless Omnipresence and countless real units. Chit (Consciousness) Pure awareness, identical to the inner Self; the world of names/forms is inert. Omnipresence is pervasive knowledge/condition-of-intelligibility (§1.2), but active sentience (chaitanya) belongs to the jeevan unit. Ananda (Bliss) Intrinsic nature of Brahman; sensory joy is a distorted reflection. Harmony realised within awakened jeevan — bliss as buddhi–atma harmony and humane conduct — not Brahman’s intrinsic ananda alone (§1.9).

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: The chit row sharpens the difference between seers. Advaita’s witness, once discriminated, is Brahman itself, without a second knower. MD’s knower is one of many constitutionally complete jeevan units, each capable of knowledge unfolding when awakened (§1.8). Both resist reduction of the first person to an observed brain-state. Dualism, panpsychism, hylomorphism, and other non-reductive views can share that resistance while giving different accounts of its bearer. The specific dispute here is whether irreducible awareness is one non-dual Self or many permanently distinct knowers.

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: Modern philosophy has no single parallel formula. Panpsychism makes experience fundamental, Russellian monism distinguishes physical structure from intrinsic nature, and process philosophy joins actuality with experience and becoming; none distributes being, sentience, and fulfilment in the precise Madhyasth Darshan pattern or identifies them as Advaita’s one Brahman.

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: 5.7 Advaita structural fork: analogues and unmappable categories

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: Advaita Vedanta and Madhyasth Darshan arise from different core commitments — non-dualism and co-existentialism — yet share portions of an Indian philosophical vocabulary. Four terms permit limited functional comparison; they are not close ontological equivalents. Several further categories required by Advaita have no Madhyasth counterpart. Advaita gives no independent absolute being to world or individual plurality, whereas Madhyasth Darshan affirms real distinct jeevan and perpetual coexistence.

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: The four analogue pairs, before the detail in §§5.7.1–5.7.4:

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: Advaita category Madhyasth Darshan analogue Shared ground Where they diverge Brahman Satta (Omnipresence) Formless, all-pervasive, non-transforming, timeless, actionless Brahman is the sole absolute reality (world mithya); Satta coexists with real nature (§5.7.1) Atman / Paramatman Jeevan (immortal sentient unit; atma as nucleus) Both deny that the conscious principle is reducible to the gross body One universal non-dual Self vs. many permanently distinct, active jeevan units (§5.7.2) Conditioned jiva Deluded or bhramit jeevan Embodied selfhood involves ignorance and body-identification Advaita denies final individuality; MD treats individuality as real and corrects its understanding (§5.7.3) Jagat / name-form Nature / units (prakriti / ikai) The physical universe of change, bodies, name, and form Jagat is ultimately mithya and sublated vs. jagat is satat — perpetual and eternally real (§5.7.4)

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: Categories Advaita needs with no Madhyasth counterpart — Maya, adhyasa, mithya, Ishvara as Brahman associated with Maya, and liberation as non-dual knowledge — are treated separately in §5.7.5; forcing them into the table above would misstate an asymmetry as a parallel.

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: The shared ground is formless, all-pervasive, non-transforming, timeless, and actionless. The divergence is decisive: Advaita’s Brahman is the sole absolute reality (paramartha), making the world dependent appearance (mithya); Madhyasth Darshan’s Satta coexists with nature (prakriti), both real. Brahman is awareness itself (chit); Satta is actionless energy (kriya-shunya urja) — the condition of intelligibility — while active sentience (chaitanya) belongs exclusively to the jeevan unit (§1.2).

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: The limited commonality is negative: neither tradition identifies the conscious principle with the gross body. Advaita holds that the true Self (Atman) is non-dual Brahman and never an individual substance. Madhyasth Darshan holds that jeevan units are permanently distinct, multiple, active, and individually immortal. Within jeevan, atma names the nuclear faculty of realisation — not a counterpart of Advaita’s universal Self. The analogy must therefore not begin from “the same immortal core”; the ontological bearer is precisely what differs.

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: The traditions share kosha vocabulary without sharing its ontological classification. MD distributes the five koshas across material, pranic, animal, and human living, including the fuller capacity of awakened human understanding (MVD, pp. 49–50; §1.6). This classification is distinct from both its five faculties of jeevan and its four developmental planes. Advaita instead discriminates the Self from all five sheaths of the empirical person (VC, vv. 149–153, 209–211). Neither the named koshas nor their ordering supplies a one-to-one map between the two accounts.

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: Both name the individual embodied self bound by ignorance and body-identification. In Advaita, the jivatman–Paramatman distinction operates at vyavahara through limiting adjuncts. Knowledge reveals that it never divided the Self into independently real beings (CU 6.8.7; BS 1.4.22; VC, v. 244). Ordinary bodily death leaves empirical rebirth in place; liberation ends ignorance without producing a new identity (§§2.6, 2.9). For MD, awakening resolves delusion while preserving the active, distinct individuality of jeevan.

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: Both point to the physical universe of change, bodies, name, and form. In Advaita, the Jagat is ultimately mithya and sublated at the highest realisation. In Madhyasth Darshan, the world of units is satat (perpetual) and eternally real.

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: The same fork appears when Advaita’s three tiers of reality (satta-traividhya) are set beside Madhyasth Darshan’s three truths (teen satya). The mark of the Advaita tiers is sublation (badha): higher knowledge withdraws the lower as not finally real. The mark of the three truths is complementarity: realisation does not cancel the unit or its relations; it makes their harmony in coexistence evident.

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: Question Advaita: three tiers Madhyasth Darshan: three truths What is counted? Apparent, empirical, and absolute reality (pratibhasika, vyavaharika, paramarthika) Inherent, positional, and existential truth (vastugat, vastu-sthiti, sthiti satya) How do the levels relate? Knowledge corrects the reality attributed to an appearance The three aspects complete one another Status of the unit and world Dependent appearance, never independently absolute Real unit, real mutuality, real saturation What realisation does Removes the attribution of independent reality to the world Reveals coexistence without cancelling units

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: Several central Advaita categories have no Madhyasth equivalent because co-existentialism explicitly rejects them.

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: Later Advaita commonly describes Maya through concealment (avarana) and projection (vikshepa), while Shankara’s indispensable commitment is that name-form has no independent being and the jiva superimposes body-mind predicates on the Self (§2.5). Madhyasth Darshan has no cosmic power or substance of illusion. Ignorance (agnyan / bhrama) is a correctable absence or distortion of understanding, resolved through study, realisation, education, and conduct rather than through sublation of the world’s reality.

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: In Advaita, world and individuality are understood through superimposition (adhyasa) and effect–cause non-difference (BS 2.1.14 with Śaṅkara’s bhāṣya; §2.5). Madhyasth Darshan has no ontological superimposition. Units are saturated (samprikt) in satta: a real, non-reductive relation in which units are active while satta remains actionless (§1.2; SB, pp. 57, 62, 69). “Mutual” must not imply reciprocal action by satta. Nor should Advaita adhyasa be confused with Madhyasth Darshan’s homonym in the animal order — species-traditional inertial impression from gestation (§1.6; SB, pp. 62–63).

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: Advaita’s mithya describes the world’s dependent status: neither independently absolute nor sheer non-being (CU 6.2.1–6.2.2 with Śaṅkara’s bhāṣya; VC, v. 251; §§2.4–2.5). Madhyasth Darshan rejects this intermediate status. Existence and real units are not annihilated, while compositions and forms arise, transform, and decompose. “Perpetual” therefore applies to coexistence and the underlying reality of units, not to every configuration or body.

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: In Advaita, Ishvara is Brahman associated with Maya and taught at vyavahara as the non-different material and efficient cause (abhinna-nimitta-upadana-karana) of name-form, not a creator ex nihilo (§§2.5–2.6). Madhyasth Darshan rejects a cosmic governor or efficient creator who plans the world or dispenses its order. That is not rejection of a pervasive ground: MVD’s “Reality” list includes “God is omnipresent, deities are many” (MVD p. 13), where God names actionless Omnipresence and no deity is elevated into the ultimate maker. Orderliness (vyavastha) is self-regulation (swatah-saspurt) in the coexisting orders (§1.6.1); satta remains kriya-shunya.

passages.heading: 5-comparison
passages.text: Advaita seeks moksha: recognition of the ever-established identity of Atman and Brahman, in which separate individuality is known never to have been absolute (CU 6.8.7; BS 1.1.4, 1.4.22). MD’s awakened coexistence preserves distinct knowers and real relationships. Shared vocabulary therefore locates a disagreement about what knowledge reveals; it does not remove that disagreement.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: 6. Critical Review

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: The comparison raises three kinds of question: whether each account is internally coherent, whether its sources support the synthesis presented here, and what reasons favour it over alternatives. Textual support answers the second question; it does not by itself answer the other two.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: 6.1 Internal coherence of the Madhyasth Darshan position

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: MD connects coexistence, real units, beginninglessness, sentience, and fulfilment in one account. Its world-realism preserves the ontological weight of nature and relationships, while its definition of human dharma as happiness and its account of value connect understanding to humane conduct (§§1.3, 1.13.1, 1.15). These are more substantial premises than the bare statement that things coexist.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: The distinction between an enduring bearer and a changing configuration also makes bodily death intelligible within the system without requiring annihilation of existence. Whether this establishes the persistence and personal continuity of a particular jeevan remains a further question (§§1.4, 1.7.1, 6.2.2).

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: These are strengths within the system’s premises. They do not by themselves establish those premises against Advaita or competing modern ontologies (§§6.2–6.4).

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: 6.2 Open problems for Madhyasth Darshan

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: The principal open questions concern identifying jeevan, explaining persistence and embodiment, relating evidence standards to scientific history, and justifying the connection between existence and obligation.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan gives a definite account of the sentience threshold. An evolving-constitution atom remains under molecular and weight bondage; through contraction and expansion it becomes free from those bondages, its particle constitution closes, and it becomes the hope-bound sentient atom called jeevan (MVD, p. 91; SB, pp. 55, 59, 114). The primary texts locate sentience in constitutionally complete jeevan, not in biological complexity alone. Omnipresence remains actionless; the knower is jeevan. The darshan locates a qualitative transition within development in the atom and distinguishes it from the compositional progression that produces molecules, cells, and bodies (§§1.7–1.8).

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: This is a specific ontological proposal. Its open evidential problem is that the texts do not provide a public procedure for identifying the proposed closed particle constitution, release from weight bondage, or hope-bondage in contemporary physical terms. A resemblance to thresholds in emergentism or integrated-information theories does not establish identity: those theories locate their thresholds in organised systems (§§3.3, 4.6). The question is what observation could distinguish constitutional completeness from the capacities already attributed to a living physical system.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: The physics vocabulary also needs an explicit interpretation. The source places electromagnetic, gravitational, weak, strong, and mediative forces alongside the sentient faculties (SB, pp. 84–85), while distinguishing imaging from motion and pressure (SB, pp. 251–252). A literal physical correspondence requires measurable quantities, units, and discriminating predictions. An analogy requires a stated common relation and a limit to the correspondence. Calling every difficult passage metaphorical would remove a claim the source may intend; treating familiar names as established physical identities would assert more than has been shown.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Quantity conservation alone does not establish personal survival: a quantity such as charge may be conserved while an organised system loses its identity. MD’s case adds constitutional completeness: the closed constitution no longer gains or loses particles and is free from molecular and weight bondage (MVD, p. 91; SB, pp. 55, 59, 114). Its statement that jeevan continues after bodily death and can work through another body presupposes this account (JV, PDF pp. 20, 55; printed pp. 19, 54). Persistence follows within MD from this further premise, rather than from a generic conservation law (§§1.7.1, 1.9).

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: The broader argument from saturation has a related limit. The source connects non-annihilation with the fact that every fragment remains saturated when a unit is divided (SB, p. 57). Continued saturation of fragments supports their presence within coexistence; it does not, by itself, prove that no entity could cease to exist or that a composite retains its identity after division. The doctrine of perpetual existence and its proposed justification therefore need to be distinguished.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Even if an enduring constitution is granted, individuation remains a separate question: what makes this jeevan this individual? The role of sanskar, memory, and personal history must be clarified, including which continuities persist across bodily death and which would count as evidence of the same individual. Equal constitutional capacities do not supply a complete criterion of personal identity.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: The remaining question is whether this persisting unit and its reassociation can be independently evidenced. Madhyasth Darshan describes the human as a joint form: the body is a material instrument, jeevan is the sentient seer–doer–enjoyer, and the two operate together through the body’s nervous and sensory organisation (MVD, pp. 115, 288–289; SB, pp. 91–92). The account distinguishes two sources of limitation. An animal body, or an impaired human nervous system, constrains what can be expressed through the bodily medium; it does not imply an incomplete jeevan. A normally developed human body supplies the provision for complete understanding, but body-identification and the resulting organisation around sensitivity leave only four and a half activities effectively evidenced until knowing and believing guide recognition and fulfilment (JV, pp. 73–74, 92–94).

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Since jeevan is described as an atom rather than a Cartesian non-physical substance, the issue should not be prejudged as an injection of energy from outside nature. Yet the texts do not translate transmission between jeevan and the nervous system into measurements that distinguish it from a brain-only account. Causal closure, organismal and psychological criteria of persistence, and the loss of measurable personal function at death all bear on this question (§§3.1, 3.4, 4.5). The missing evidence concerns how bodily impairment constrains expression, what difference jeevan makes to bodily activity, and what could establish post-death continuity.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: MD expects understanding to become publicly evident through resolution, justice, mutual fulfilment, and participation in orderliness (MVD, pp. 88, 115; SB, p. 44; §§1.14, 5.3.5). This is a substantial practical evidence standard. Its relation to ontological evidence still needs explanation: how does evidence of humane conduct discriminate the proposed constitution of jeevan from rival accounts that also permit such conduct? Logical argument, first-person verification, conduct, and instrument-based measurement can inform one another without functioning as interchangeable tests.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: The apparent conflict between niyati-kram and evolutionary contingency also needs narrowing. MD’s progression names an ordered relation among material, bio, animal, and knowledge orders, while evolutionary biology explains branching changes within living populations through variation, inheritance, selection, drift, development, and contingency (§§1.6, 4.4). These claims are not direct contradictories merely because one uses definite order language and the other uses contingency: they operate at different descriptive levels. The sharper questions are whether MD requires each transition to occur necessarily, how its compositional claims map onto biological descent, and what evidence would distinguish a necessary existential progression from a retrospective classification of the forms that happened to arise. Until that mapping is supplied, niyati-kram remains a distinctive commitment of the darshan rather than a result established by evolutionary science.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: MD’s case for humane conduct combines several premises: human dharma is happiness; value expresses essentiality and fulfilled participation; and understanding identifies definite expectations in relationships (§§1.3, 1.13.1, 1.15). Coexistence by itself would establish only that things exist together, not what a person ought to do. The normative argument depends on those fuller claims about human fulfilment and the conditions under which it is realised.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: The critical questions are therefore whether those premises are independently defensible, how they distinguish beneficial participation from harmful but causally effective activity, and how disagreements over actual fulfilment are resolved. Evidence in conduct is relevant to this task, but it must assess the relationship and its result rather than assume that every naturally occurring relation is already humane. The detailed argument belongs to Axiology: Value Theory.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: 6.3 Advaita — strengths and limits

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Advaita combines ontological economy with a developed account of error and liberation. Its argument against existence arising from non-existence (CU 6.2.2), seer-seen discrimination, and analysis of waking, dream, and deep sleep address different aspects of the relation between experience and reality. Empirical ethics, loka-sangraha, and beginningless cosmology give the world practical and explanatory standing (§§2.1–2.10).

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: MD’s principal objection concerns the ultimate status of that world. It requires distinct knowers and real relationships to remain at the highest understanding, whereas Advaita denies ultimate separateness. That is a substantive disagreement in premises; failure to reproduce MD’s categories is not itself an internal contradiction in Advaita. Nagraj frames the origination question directly:

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: “How can the jeeva and jagat, which originated from the Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite Brahma, be an illusion?” - MVD, The Alternative

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: This question concerns how a world dependent on Brahman can lack independent reality. It is related to, but not identical with, later controversies about the locus of ignorance. The quoted objection alone does not establish an engagement with a particular later school’s solution.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Advaita’s reply distinguishes empirical causal instruction from ultimate non-duality: name-form never had independent being apart from Brahman (BS 2.1.14; §§2.4–2.6). It does not claim that Brahman manufactured a second independently real world and later made it unreal. The remaining dispute is whether the arguments for sublation warrant giving plurality this dependent status, and whether empirical reality adequately grounds the continuing significance of relationships. MD answers the second question by retaining ultimate plurality; Advaita rejects the demand that responsibility at vyavahara requires such plurality. Comparing those answers requires examining their reasons for the distinction between empirical and ultimate reality, not merely counting their fundamental entities.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: 6.4 Modern approaches — strengths and limits

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Strengths.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Scientific approaches are strongest where Madhyasth Darshan is least operational: public measurement, empirical correction, cognitive modelling, and precise mechanism. Self-model theory and predictive processing explain embodied selfhood and regulation without requiring an eternal jeevan (§4.5), while consciousness programs expose distinct predictions to comparative testing (§4.6).

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Contemporary philosophy adds conceptual pressure from several sides rather than one physicalist front. Causal exclusion, animalism, panpsychist combination, hylomorphic embodiment, and processual persistence each test a different MD commitment. Scientific realism aligns with MD on mind-independent nature, but only on that question (§5.3.2).

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Open limits.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: The hard problem remains: correlation of brain and experience is not disputed, but why physical processing is accompanied by subjectivity remains open (§3.2), and rival consciousness programs lack consensus (§4.6). That is not proof of jeevan; it marks an explanatory burden for reductive accounts and a branching point among several non-reductive alternatives.

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Non-reductive alternatives face their own identifying and explanatory tasks: subject-combination for micropsychism, individuation for cosmopsychism, and the relation between an enduring bearer and embodied activity for soul theories. These are distinct problems; their existence does not make all alternatives equally supported (§§3.3–3.6).

passages.heading: 6-critical-review
passages.text: Modern scientific and philosophical approaches therefore supply indispensable mechanisms and public tests without yet delivering a single settled ontology of consciousness or selfhood. Predictive models explain aspects of bodily regulation and self-experience but do not by themselves settle the ontological bearer; an explanatory gap is not an existence proof for jeevan, and a successful mechanism is not automatically a complete metaphysics.

passages.heading: 7-conclusion
passages.text: 7. Conclusion

passages.heading: 7-conclusion
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan’s distinctive claim is coexistence: formless Omnipresence (satta) and countless real units (ikai), beginningless and neither made from the other. The plural world remains real in its own right.

passages.heading: 7-conclusion
passages.text: “Brahma is truth, the world is perpetual.” - MVD, p. 13

passages.heading: 7-conclusion
passages.text: MD connects this world-realism to a distinct sentient bearer and an account of fulfilment. Units retain definite constitutions and capacities; their properties, usefulness, and participation become evident in mutuality. Human knowing can understand that order or mis-evaluate it. Awakening is fulfilled when understanding regulates conduct and supports mutually fulfilled relationships.

passages.heading: 7-conclusion
passages.text: The comparison locates both agreements and decisive differences. Scientific realism also affirms mind-independent nature, but does not establish perpetual units or actionless satta. Advaita and several non-reductive philosophies resist reducing experience to a physical description, but disagree about the number, constitution, and persistence of its bearers. In Advaita, empirical rebirth is compatible with ultimate non-duality; in MD, awakening preserves distinct jeevan. These differences remain after shared vocabulary is clarified.

passages.heading: 7-conclusion
passages.text: Further work must address public identification of constitutional completeness and the interpretation of physical vocabulary (§6.2.1); individuation, persistence, and joint operation with a body (§6.2.2); the relation between conduct evidence, scientific measurement, and evolutionary history (§6.2.3); and the premises connecting coexistence to obligation (§6.2.4). The primary texts support a connected ontology. Establishing its claims against alternatives requires further argument and evidence at these points.

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Appendix: Quick Glossary

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Key terms introduced in §§1–4 and used in the §5 comparison are collected here for quick reference. Each term is also defined where it first appears in the exposition.

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Terms in §1

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Term Plain meaning Coexistence (saha-astitva) Reality as the pervasive ground (satta) and all units (ikai) inseparably present together — beginningless, without creation from nothing. Satta (Omnipresence) The formless, all-pervasive, non-transforming ground in which all units are saturated. See Editorial Notes on translation conventions. Unit (ikai) A countable, bounded entity in nature—insentient (jada) or sentient (chaitanya). The atom is the root unit; a molecule, cell, body, or planet may be treated as a composite unit while its definite composition and conduct persist. A body–jeevan joint form and a human assembly are coordinated wholes of other kinds (§§1.1, 1.5, 1.13.3). Unithood (ikaitva) is the abstract form: being a bounded unit at all, which together with energy-fullness is activeness (§1.2). Form (roop) Shape, volume, and density: the real framework and boundary of a unit. The constituted unit is imaged in mutual facing (§1.3). Object, image, imaging (bimb, pratibimb, pratibimban) The unit in its constituted configuration, its image in mutual facing, and its being imaged. Imaging provides the basis of recognition in mutuality, including insentient mutuality (§1.3). Light / manifestness (jyoti, prakash, prakashmanata) Omnipresence is also named Light (jyoti), connected with the eternal light of realisation in it. Units are manifest (prakashman) through saturation, with form, properties, essential nature, and dharma. Prakash also names imaging in mutuality; its contextual meanings are distinguished in Editorial Notes (§§1.1–1.3). Presentation, communication, expression (prakashan, sampreshana, abhivyakti) Connected aspects of manifestness according to state, motion, plane, and order. In sentient life these include bodily expression and the communication of capacity; in awakened human living they fulfil meaningful presentation of actuality, indication of completeness, and mental, verbal, and bodily activity for all-round resolution (§§1.3, 1.14). Property / property-endowed (guna / guni) Guni is the force-bearing unit and guna its inseparable relative power, effective as generative, degenerative, or mediative influence when units come together (§1.3). Essential nature (svabhav) Essentiality or the usefulness of guna, expressed and recognised according to state, motion, plane, order, and the particular mutuality (§§1.3, 1.13.1, 1.6). Dharma (unit innateness) What is inseparable from an underlying unit and fulfilled through its order: existence, with growth, hope to live, and happiness cumulatively stated in higher orders. A composite form may disintegrate without its constituents becoming non-existent. Distinct from the human dharma–adharma evaluative perspective (§§1.3, 1.13.2, 1.4). Mutual facing (sammukhata) The unit–unit relation in which imaging and recognition occur. Imaging and the influences of relative powers are distinguished within the wider account of mutuality (§1.3). Saturation (sampriktata) The ever-present bond in which each unit is soaked, submerged, and surrounded in Omnipresence. Energy-fullness, forcefulness, activeness, manifestness, recognition, and regulation belong to this inseparable condition. Their connections are ontological, not stages in time or an explicitly described physical mechanism (§1.2). Three truths (teen satya) Inherent truth of the unit (vastugat satya), positional truth in mutuality (vastu-sthiti satya), and existential truth as nature saturated in Omnipresence (sthiti satya). Complementary aspects, not three worlds and not Advaita’s three tiers (§1.3; §5.7.4). Effort–motion–result (shram–gati–parinam) The inseparable triad of unit-activity. Its developmental goals are immortality of result at constitutional completeness, restfulness of effort at activity completeness, and destination of motion at conduct completeness. The overlapping relations to the four aspects are explained in §1.3 (SB pp. 58, 60–62). Immortality of result (parinam ki amarta) Constitutional completeness (T1 / gathanpurnata): particle constitution no longer increases or decreases, while qualitative activity continues (§1.7). Restfulness of effort (shram ka vishram) The teleological goal of effort (shram) at activity completeness (T2 / kriyapurnata) — internal cognitive seeking resolves into realisation and samadhan (§1.11.1). Destination of motion (gati ka gantavya) The teleological goal of motion (gati) at conduct completeness (T3 / acharanpurnata) — external behavioural participation aligned with universal orderliness (§1.11.2). The four orders (chaar avastha) Material, bio/pranic, animal, and knowledge/human — distinguishable manifestations of nature, with cumulative dharmas and definite modes of conformance (§1.6). Five koshas Capacities named annamaya, pranamaya, manomaya, anandamaya, and vigyanmaya, distributed across the four orders; distinct from the faculties and planes (§1.6). Supreme cause (mahakaran) Satta as the non-transforming sustaining condition of all unit-activity — not an efficient maker, planner, or material that becomes the units (§1.4; §5.4). Substance and form (vastu / roop) The underlying reality of a unit persists while its form or configuration changes; this is an ontological claim distinct from conservation of a measured physical quantity (§1.4; §§4.3, 5.4). Relationship (sambandh) Definite mutuality with expectations predetermined toward completeness (MVD p. 62). Contact (sampark) Mutuality whose particular expectations are voluntary; it remains subject to justice and responsibility (§1.13.1). Law (ontological) Orderliness and regulation read from saturation — universal across all four orders; not statutory command. Sanskar / sanskar-conformance Acquired acceptances and dispositions, and human conduct according to them. They may reproduce delusion or support awakening (§1.6.1). Universal orderliness (vyavastha) Participation of units and orders in definite, mutually fulfilling relations; in human life it becomes evident through resolved conduct, not merely physical regularity (§§1.13.1, 1.6.1, 1.15). Perpetual world (jagat satat) The claim that the world and coexistence remain real through transformation; it does not mean that every body or configuration is permanent (§1.4; §5.3.2). Jeevan The sentient self: a constitutionally complete, immortal unit — atma as nucleus, buddhi–mun as orbital structure — that works through the body (§1.8). Bodily medium The sensory and nervous organisation through which jeevan expresses its activities. The brain (medhas) receives and translates signals between jeevan and the body. Animal bodies constrain expression to hope-bound species-conformance; the fully enriched human nervous system provides for complete understanding (§§1.6, 1.8). Comprehension (bodh) The reflective activity of buddhi: understanding coexistence, not a mystical flash of light (§1.8). Direct apprehension (sakshatkar) The reflective activity of chitta: recognising the known without constructing it (§1.8). Reflection (pratyavartan) The inward knowing direction of jeevan’s activities, through which the manifest world is understood. Distinct from imaging (pratibimban) in mutual facing (§§1.3, 1.8). Tasting (asvadan) The reflective activity of mun: accepting what is relished. It has sensory, value-based, and goal-based forms (ruchi-mulak, mulya-mulak, lakshya-mulak) (§1.8). Higher- / lower-conformance Purvanukram is guidance descending from atma to mun; paranukram is sensory drive pushing inward (MVD pp. 207–208; §1.8). Delusion (bhram) In human living, jeevan’s identification of itself with the body and the resulting organisation of evaluation around bodily sensitivity rather than known actuality (§§1.11.1, 1.8). Sanvedansheelta / sangyansheelta Sensitivity through the body and senses, and cognisance of relationship, value, and orderliness through jeevan. Awakened living balances them by regulating sensitivity through understanding (§1.8). Constitutional completeness (gathanpurnata) When a developed atom integrates its required particles and crosses irreversibly into sentient jeevan (Transition 1, T1). Existential progression (niyati-kram) Definite order of material, pranic, animal, and knowledge manifestations under conducive conditions; not a timetable or a claim that each instance advances (§1.12). Way of existence (niyati-vidhi) Definiteness in the conduct of each of the four orders; paired with niyati-kram (order emergence ↔ order conduct; §1.6.1). Development progression (vikas-kram) Atomic-level movement through the physicochemical complex until an atom reaches constitutional completeness and sentient jeevan appears (§1.12). Awakening progression (jagriti-kram) Sentient-level movement within constitutionally complete jeevan toward fuller activity and conduct (§1.12). Padmukti Release from incomplete developmental standing in the divine or complete condition; jeevan continues to exist (§1.12.2). Prarabdha Results still to be undergone within the relation between knowing, desiring, doing, and enjoying (§1.10). Gross, subtle, causal, supreme cause Compositions and bodies, atoms, atma, and satta, respectively; different from the Advaita three-body account (§1.14). Jeevan values (sukh, shanti, santosh, anand) Four harmonies within jeevan — happiness, peace, contentment, bliss — each borne as a named activity by the outer faculty of its pair (§1.9). Object-value family Usefulness and art or aesthetic value; two object values within the thirty-value canon (§1.13.1). Utility value (upyogita) What an object can fulfil through its definite properties. Changing price does not change that function; material condition and conditions of use can change actual fulfilment (JV p. 123; §1.13.1). Art (kala) / art value (kala-mulya) Kala makes qualities evident and expression meaningful, joining usefulness and beauty. Art value names its useful and aesthetic accomplishment in an object; the activity also serves the presentation and communication of understanding (§§1.13.1, 1.14; PS p. 56). Human values The six values of fortitude, courage, generosity, kindness, grace, and compassion through which humaneness is evidenced (§§1.13.1, 1.6). Established values The nine relationship values—trust, respect, affection, care, guidance, reverence, glory, gratitude, and love—borne at chitta, vritti, and mun and flowing when relationships are recognised (MAD reader p. 30; JV pp. 108, 138; §1.13.1). Expressed values (shishta-mulya) The nine powers in motion paired with the established values. MVD’s English translation renders them civic values; they are relationship-expression, not a separate civic family of body-mind-wealth use (Paribhasha pp. 151, 154; §1.13.1). Thirty values (tees mulya) Four jeevan, six human, nine established, nine expressed, and two object values across realisation, thought, behaviour, and work (Paribhasha pp. 151, 154; §1.13.1). Gyan / vivek / vigyan Knowledge, wisdom, and science: knowing reality, recognising the goals of living, and determining how means serve those goals. Gyan also names the actionless pervasive ground; context distinguishes ground, understood content, and the knower’s activity (§1.14; Editorial Notes). Value, character, ethics The content of humane fulfilment, definite humane conduct, and policies supporting humaneness; together they constitute the account of humane conduct (§1.13.3). Evaluative domain Conduct, thought, or realisation — the three humane perspectives discipline distinct domains (§1.13.2). Sentient mode How effort–motion–result maps once constitutional completeness is reached — distinct from insentient unit-activity (§§1.10–1.11).

passages.text: Further terms — planes, justice, prosperity — are defined where they first appear in §1.

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Terms in §2

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Term Plain meaning Brahman The sole absolute reality — being, consciousness, and limitless fullness or bliss (sat-chit-ananda), one without a second; ananda here is not a passing pleasurable state (§2.2). Nirguna Attribute-free Brahman at paramartha — actionless, not an object among objects. Saguna Brahman associated with Maya and spoken of as Ishvara — operative at vyavahara. Atman and jiva Atman is the non-dual Self, identical with Brahman; jiva or jivatman is that Self appearing as an embodied individual through limiting adjuncts at vyavahara. Ishvara and jagat Ishvara is Brahman associated with Maya, taught as the non-different material and efficient cause (abhinna-nimitta-upadana-karana) of name-form; jagat is that shared world of name-form, empirically valid but not independently absolute (§2.6). Paramartha Absolute level of truth; Brahman alone is absolutely real. Vyavahara Shared empirical order of bodies, law, ethics, and scripture; valid for living without being independently absolute. Pratibhasika Apparent error (rope-snake, dream objects); sublated by correction or waking. Mithya Dependent appearance, neither independently absolute nor sheer nothing; its attributed independent reality is sublated by knowledge. Badha Sublation: correction of the reality attributed to an appearance; knowledge does not turn a previously independent world into an unreal one (§2.4). Maya Name for the empirical principle through which name-form is taught; later Advaita commonly analyses it as concealment (avarana) and projection (vikshepa). Avidya Ignorance and superimposition of body-mind predicates on the Self; its precise relation to Maya is disputed in later Advaita. Adhyasa Superimposition: cognition of something in that which it is not; mutual placement of Self and not-self (BS, Adhyasa Bhashya). Distinct from MD bhram, which is evaluative misidentification of a real body (§2.5). Adhishthana Substrate of an appearance: the rope in the rope-snake error, and Brahman in the account of dependent name-form (§2.5). Anirvacaniya-khyati Later Advaita theory of error: the object of error is indescribable as real or unreal (§2.5). Adhyaropa–apavada Provisional attribution then withdrawal — teaching by admitting name-form and later negating it. Effect–cause non-difference The effect has no independent being apart from its cause (CU 6.1.4; BS 2.1.14). Vivartavada Later Advaita term for apparent rather than real transformation; Brahman remains changeless while name-form appears at vyavahara. Parinama Real transformation of a cause into its effect; used as the contrast against vivarta, not adopted as Advaita’s account of Brahman’s relation to the world (§§2.5, 5.4). Upadhi Limiting adjunct conditioning the Self (body, mind, sheaths). Pratibimba / Avaccheda Reflection and limitation — classical accounts of how one Self appears as many jivas under adjuncts. Sthula / Sukshma / Karana Gross, subtle, and causal bodies in the empirical account of embodiment; the subtle body carries capacities and impressions across births (§2.6). Antahkarana Internal organ whose functions are distinguished as mind (manas), determination (buddhi), embodied self-identification (ahamkara), and memory (chitta); illuminated by the Self rather than independently conscious (§2.6). Pancha kosha Five sheaths (food, vital, mental, intellect, bliss) conditioning the embodied self at vyavahara. Srishti–sthiti–laya Manifestation, maintenance, and dissolution — beginningless empirical cycles, not a single absolute beginning. Turiya The non-dual Self or awareness in which waking, dream, and deep sleep appear; called the “fourth,” but not a fourth experiential state alongside the other three. Sakshin / Svaprakasha Witness and self-luminosity: the Self reveals objects and mental states without requiring a second awareness to reveal it; witness-language does not imply ultimate subject–object duality (§2.7). Ajati Non-origination at the absolute standpoint: no independently real birth or becoming of Brahman; distinguished from empirical causal explanation (§2.8). Moksha Liberation — recognition of pre-existing identity with Brahman, not merger of a real individual. Jivanmukti / Videhamukti Liberating knowledge while embodied, and the ending of bodily continuation when already-begun karma is exhausted; bodily death does not complete knowledge (§2.9). Karma / Samsara Empirical continuity of the conditioned person across births until knowledge dispels separateness. Shabda and the knowledge path Upanishadic testimony, understood through hearing (shravana), reasoning (manana), and sustained contemplation (nididhyasana), is Advaita’s distinctive means for knowing non-dual Brahman (§2.9). Loka-sangraha and prarabdha Loka-sangraha is action for holding the world together and guiding others; prarabdha is already-begun karmic momentum under which embodied life continues after knowledge (§2.10).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Terms in §3

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Term Plain meaning Physicalism The family of views that every concrete phenomenon is physical or wholly physically realised; reductive, functional, and non-reductive versions differ. Weak emergence can remain physicalist, while strong emergence may posit powers not admitted by standard physicalism. Methodological naturalism A rule of inquiry seeking publicly testable explanations without invoking non-natural interventions; it is not itself the metaphysical thesis that only the physical exists. Causal closure The thesis that every physical event has a sufficient physical cause; important in exclusion arguments but not the definition of every physicalism (Kim 2005). Hard problem Why and how physical processes give rise to subjective experience — the “something it is like” (Chalmers 1995; Nagel 1974). Property and substance dualism Property dualism treats conscious properties as irreducible even if dependent on physical systems; substance dualism posits a distinct mental bearer. Both face interaction or dependence questions. Panpsychism A family treating experience or proto-experience as fundamental, including micropsychism, panprotopsychism, and cosmopsychism. It can combine with Russellian monism but is not identical with it. Russellian monism The view that physics reveals relational or dispositional structure while leaving the intrinsic nature of its bearers open; that intrinsic basis may be construed experientially or proto-experientially, but need not be. Combination / decombination problem How many micro-subjects could constitute one macro-subject, or how local subjects derive from a cosmic subject. Emergence The appearance of higher-level properties from organised lower-level systems; weak emergence preserves physical dependence, while strong emergence claims irreducible causal powers. Illusionism Denies phenomenal properties as ordinarily conceived while explaining access, discrimination, self-report, and why experience seems to possess those properties (Frankish 2016). Personal identity What makes a person persist — the organism (animalism), psychological continuity, material constitution, narrative or embodied agency, or an enduring substance. Scientific realism The philosophical view that successful mature science gives approximate knowledge of a mind-independent world, including unobservables. Instrumentalism / constructive empiricism Interpretations that restrict commitment to predictive success or empirical adequacy rather than treating every successful theoretical entity as part of a final ontology. Hylomorphism / process metaphysics Hylomorphism understands concrete substances through matter organised by form; process metaphysics takes becoming and relation, rather than static substance alone, as ontologically basic. Monad Leibniz’s simple, partless substance, with perception and internally unfolding states; coordinated with other monads by pre-established harmony (§3.6.3). Berkeleyan idealism Active spirits perceive passive ideas; sensible objects depend on perception, with their regular order grounded in divine agency (§3.6.6). Neutral monism Mind and matter are composed of a common neutral stuff, neither mental nor material in isolation (Russell 1921; Mach 1914). Samadhanatmak bhautikvad Resolution Centred Materialism — MD’s reframing of materialism: real matter saturated in Omnipresence, not consciousness-from-matter or matter-only reduction (SB).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Scientific realism, structural realism, instrumentalism, and constructive empiricism offer competing interpretations of what successful science warrants. The metaphysical families above also contain internally diverse positions (§§3.1–3.7).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Terms in §4

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Term Plain meaning Science Publicly corrigible inquiry through observation, instrumentation, modelling, intervention, replication, and criticism. Its findings constrain ontologies without by themselves selecting physicalism or another complete metaphysics (§§3.1, 4.1). Self-model A representation of embodied organism, perspective, agency, and continuity maintained by a cognitive system — not by itself evidence of an immortal unit or a complete theory of personal identity (Metzinger 2003). Predictive processing A family of hierarchical generative-model accounts in which perception and learning depend on prediction, prediction error, and precision; it is related to but not identical with active inference. Active inference A framework connecting generative models to action and policy selection under variational free energy, including regulation that keeps an organism within viable bounds (Friston 2010; Clark 2016). Integrated information IIT 4.0’s irreducible cause–effect structure, developed from proposed phenomenal properties; not merely a numerical self-threshold (Albantakis et al. 2023). Competing consciousness theories Global neuronal workspace theory emphasises global availability and broadcast; higher-order theories require representation of a mental state as one’s own; recurrent-processing theory locates a key condition in recurrent sensory activity. None is presently a settled winner (§4.6). Autopoiesis Living organisation as a self-producing metabolic network; not by itself a theory of consciousness (Maturana and Varela 1980). ΛCDM Standard cosmological model describing an early hot dense epoch and subsequent observable history; not a proof of absolute creation. Quantum field Dynamical physical field whose quantised excitations can appear as particles; fields themselves are not “conserved entities” (Weinberg 1995). Brain death / DNC Brain death or death by neurologic criteria: determination of death through specified neurological criteria in the cited clinical guideline; not an independent test of non-physical survival (§4.5). Entropy Statistical quantity related to the multiplicity of microscopic states compatible with a macroscopic description; “disorder” is only a rough metaphor. Natural selection Differential persistence and reproduction of heritable variation, operating with drift, development, ecology, and other evolutionary processes.
