passages.text: Editorial Notes

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Scope, text editions, and pagination conventions

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The principal translated base is Madhyasth Darshan — Co-existentialism (MVD), Samadhanatmak Bhautikvad (Resolution Centred Materialism, SB), and Jeevan Vidya: An Introduction (JV). Their page references use one-based positions in the linked PDFs; JV’s printed page is one below that position. Paribhasha Samhita (PS) uses printed pages, eight below PDF position; Manav Abhyas Darshan (MAD) uses displayed native-reader pages. Manav Karm Darshan (KD) is used through the Hindi text and an identified working-English paraphrase where the Hindi has been checked. Its section numbers and printed pages are specified where used.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Full knowability is treated in The Epistemology of Coexistence §7.1; time, trikaalabadh, and spacetime in Nature of Time; and institutional governance, dharma-niti, rajya-niti, and statutory order in the planned Governance Justice and Undivided Society. How to Form Self-Sustaining Organizations applies the assembly template socially.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: English translations and names for satta (vyapak)

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The translations alternate “Omnipotence” and “Omnipresence” for the same all-pervasive reality, satta; vyapak means all-pervasive. This study uses “Omnipresence” in analytical prose to avoid the theistic implications of “Omnipotence”; quotations retain their source wording. The translated “Space” renders shunya, formless emptiness, rather than physical akasha.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Uniform Energy, Knowledge, Consciousness, Eternity, God, and Absolute Energy also name this reality (SB p. 48). Their meaning follows the relations explained at MVD p. 35: bliss through realisation, truth through uniform realisability, supreme reality through conservation and regulation, pervasiveness through uniform presence, consciousness in relation to sentient nature, and absolute energy through saturated units’ activity. Completeness names the ground’s absence of transformation. Absolute and relative energy are distinguished at MVD p. 40. PS p. 137 lists jyoti alongside pervasive reality, uniform satta, knowledge, and consciousness under Brahm; PS p. 80 defines jyoti through experience in the pervasive as eternal light. The account of satta as light in §1.1 is a synthesis of these connected uses, not a quotation of an unqualified definition equating satta with every meaning of prakash.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: These names do not attribute a knowing mind, personal will, measurable physical energy, or physical extension to the ground. In particular, “(consciousness)” at SB p. 48 names satta, while active sentience belongs to jeevan. Gyan likewise names both the actionless ground (MVD p. 35) and knowledge as understood content. The study retains these contextual uses: jeevan knows coexistence, itself, and humane conduct; gyan-avastha names the human order capable of knowing. The related roles of gyan, vivek, and vigyan follow MVD p. 170 (§1.14). This distinction governs the comparison with Advaita’s chit (§§5.6, 5.7.1).

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Saturation, manifestness, and imaging formulations

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The saturation formulations overlap. SB p. 57 associates being soaked with forcefulness, submerged with activeness, and surrounded with regulation; PS p. 114 associates them with energy-endowment, mutual recognition, and regulation. §1.2 preserves these connections without assigning each description one exclusive consequence. Permeation in units and transparency in mutuality (MVD p. 32) connect with recognising images (PS p. 114); force-endowment in saturation grounds manifestness (SB p. 248). AVD pp. 115–116 explicitly connects the permeation of insentient and sentient nature by state-complete satta with units’ force-endowment, activeness, and manifestness.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Prakash is defined through imaging at MVD p. 45 and through a heated body at PS p. 119. These contexts do not exhaust the light vocabulary, which also includes jyoti as a name of the pervasive reality and the eternal light of realisation in it (PS pp. 80, 137). PS p. 119 defines prakashman through being imaged on all sides and manifest with the four aspects, and prakashmayata through imaging, properties, essential nature, and dharma in orderliness. “Manifestness” explains prakashmanata while preserving this light and imaging vocabulary; prakash, prakashman, and prakashan are not interchangeable names for intelligibility.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The constituted unit (bimb), its image (pratibimb), and imaging (pratibimban) are distinguished at PS pp. 121 and 135. SB pp. 248–252 separates imaging from properties’ effects; its distinction of imaging and prakashan from motion or pressure (p. 252) supplies no optical or information-transfer mechanism. An image provides a basis of recognition, not complete human understanding of all four aspects. “Imaging” translates pratibimban; “reflection” translates the inward knowing activity pratyavartan (§1.8). Advaita’s pratibimba has a separate explanatory role (§2.6).

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The cloth-in-water illustration in §1.2 explains the three everyday relations; it is this study’s illustration, not an attributed source example. Water is bounded material, whereas Omnipresence is formless and saturation is inseparable from every unit. Likewise, “natural” and “excited” describe order-definite activity and its displacement, rather than psychological moods.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Form, properties, essential nature, and dharma

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: “Properties” (guna) and “essential nature” (svabhav) can suggest predicates understood in isolation. Here they retain their relational definitions: relative powers and their effects, and the essentiality or usefulness of those effects (MVD p. 47). The bearer and its capacities remain real; manifested effects depend on the actual mutuality. Dharma names inseparable innateness and fulfilment. These translations preserve the distinctions among constitution, imaging, effects, usefulness, and understanding.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The reviewed passages connect constitution with activity and conduct without quantitatively deriving every guna, svabhav, or dharma from particle structure alone. The effort–motion–result correspondences overlap (SB pp. 60–62); they do not reassign the four aspects one-to-one. “Evaluation” also has different scopes: animal recognition of essential nature as friendliness or opposition (SB pp. 249–250), and human judgment of values, dharma, and resolution (§1.3).

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Value families, faculty pairings, and thirty-value enumeration

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: This study uses “contact” for sampark, occasionally rendered “association” in Gupta’s MVD translation, and “relationship” for sambandh (pp. 61–62). Contact’s particular expectations are voluntary; relationship’s expectations are predetermined toward completeness. Both carry duties of justice (MVD pp. 61, 311–312), so voluntary terms do not make justice optional.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The five families named at MVD p. 305 and JV p. 43 receive an explicit thirty-value enumeration at PS pp. 151 and 154: four jeevan, six human, nine established, nine expressed, and two object values. MAD reader p. 30 supplies the principal established–expressed pairs; illustrative wording at JV p. 108 does not replace that enumeration. Gupta’s “civic values” translates shishta-mulya; “expressed values” identifies its nine relationship expressions here and in Axiology: Value Theory §1.3. Other uses of mulya need not add members to this enumeration.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Family identifies evaluative role; faculty identifies a value’s location in jeevan (MVD pp. 328–348; AVD pp. 91–94). The AVD English appendix reverses force/power headings relative to their Hindi orientation. This study follows bal as state and shakti as motion (KD §3.8, printed p. 84), checking definitions and pairings rather than English headings alone. The inventory cited in §1.13.1 records detailed readings. Object values concern material units; each jeevan harmony is borne at the outer faculty of its pair (§1.9).

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Expressive activities and completeness transitions

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The attribution of presentation, communication, and expression to every entity follows SB p. 179 and MVD p. 109 (§1.3). Their connection with sentient manifestness follows the account of jeevan manifesting and communicating through bodily composition (SB p. 52), its active and manifest forces and powers (p. 63), and humans communicating and expressing capacity, ability, and receptivity during awakening progression (p. 66). This progression retains both general usage and developed human meaning. The fuller definitions at PS pp. 22, 119, and 206 concern awakened human activity: meaningful presentation of actuality, indication of completeness, and expression for all-round resolution (§1.14). These terms overlap: abhivyakti includes prakashan, jeevan’s activities, and bodily activity. They neither attribute human intention to insentient units nor define three successive stages of imaging.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The reviewed definitions do not assign the three terms exclusively to vritti–chitta, chitta–buddhi, and buddhi–atma. MVD p. 328 brings expression, communication, and exposition together under realisation-based ultimate bliss. Kala makes qualities evident and expression meaningful, joining usefulness and beauty (PS p. 56); kala-mulya is its object-value application.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: T1, T2, and T3 are this study’s labels for constitutional, activity, and conduct completeness. They connect result–immortality, effort–restfulness, and motion–destination (SB p. 58) with atomic development, realisation, and humane conduct. Individual completeness is distinguished from social continuity (MVD pp. 15–16); conduct completeness does not require prior universal awakening. All ten jeevan activities remain inherent; “four and a half” describes their restricted effective organisation in body-centred human living (JV pp. 73, 93–94). The three sensory perspectives and three humane perspectives explain the scope of restricted deliberation (MVD p. 67); their count is not a quantitative measurement of cognitive capacity. Bodily capacity separately limits what a joint form can express, especially in the animal order (§1.8).

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Advaita Vedanta sources, terminology, and textual conventions

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The principal basis is the Upanishads with Shankara’s authenticated commentaries, the Brahma Sutra Bhashya, and the Bhagavad Gita Bhashya. The Vivekachudamani, traditionally attributed to Shankara but of uncertain authorship, and the Drig-Drishya-Viveka, attributed variously to Shankara or Bharati Tirtha, serve pedagogical explanation rather than settling historical disputes. Gaudapada’s non-origination doctrine is cited from the Mandukya Karika with Shankara’s commentary.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Shankara’s Adhyasa Bhashya grounds the superimposition account; anirvacaniya-khyati names a later systematic error theory (§2.5). MD’s bhram concerns a real jeevan misidentifying a real body as itself; its animal-order adhyasa means gestational impression (§5.7.5). Likewise, MD’s three truths concern the unit’s aspects, its position in mutuality, and its saturation in Omnipresence (SB pp. 250–251; MVD pp. 88, 97; YAT). They are complementary, rather than Advaita’s tiers of sublation or a yatharthata / vastavikta / satyata ladder.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Mithya names dependent ontological status; tiers of validity distinguish what sublation corrects. Shankara already calls name-form indeterminable as identical with or different from Brahman (BS 1.1.5), and as real or unreal (BS 2.1.14). Later formulations of mithyatva, error, concealment/projection, and apparent transformation are distinguished from those bases. No verified first occurrence of sad-asad-anirvacaniya is claimed, nor is the complete later theory assigned to Shankara. Nagraj’s origination objection remains distinct from the later debate over ignorance’s locus (§6.3).

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The ananda comparison (§§2.2, 5.6) rests on TU 2.1’s satyam–jnanam–anantam and TU 2.7’s identification of Brahman as rasa, fullness through whose attainment one becomes blissful. TU 2.5’s bliss sheath remains an object of discrimination. Thus ananda indicates limitless completeness, rather than a passing feeling or the sheath alone.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The cited Gambhirananda Gita edition counts Arjuna’s opening question as 13.1; its field-and-knower verses 13.2–13.3 correspond to 13.1–13.2 in editions omitting that question from the count. References distinguish these conventions and, where applicable, printed pages from PDF positions.

passages.heading: references
passages.text: §1 (introduction). Existence as coexistence of Omnipresence (satta) and units of nature, insentient (jada) and sentient (chaitanya): SB pp. 48–49; MVD pp. 11, 34. Continuous seeking of happiness; four stages of happiness: MVD p. 163. Societal telos (fearlessness, prosperity, trust, undivided society): MVD p. 160 ff.; JV p. 61; §§1.15–1.16 references below.

passages.heading: references
passages.text: §1.1. Two-pole structure: “What is evident is that consciousness and matter are inseparably present. Upon examining their fundamental nature, we learn that all of existence is essentially nature (matter) saturated in Omnipotence (consciousness). Here, ‘seeing’ is intended in the sense of understanding. Since nature saturated in Omnipotence is inseparably present, existence itself is eternally manifest in the form of coexistence.” (SB, p. 48). Omnipresence as actionless energy (kriya-shunya urja), ground of energising, regulation, conservation: SB pp. 48–49. English names for satta (Omnipotence, Uniform Energy, Space / shunya, Knowledge / gyan, Consciousness, Absolute Energy): SB p. 48. Units bounded from six directions; form, property, essential nature, and dharma as inseparable aspects: SB p. 48; MVD pp. 11, 34. Source explanations of the names for satta: MVD p. 35. Jyoti among the names for Brahm alongside uniform satta, and its definition through experience in the pervasive as eternal light: PS pp. 80, 137. Atom as root of physical, chemical, and jeevan activity; nucleus and orbits as root quantity: KD 3.1; MVD pp. 42, 78, 149. Separation “never happens”: SB p. 70; JV p. 18. No absent place: SB pp. 48, 62, 69. Inter-unit distance held in satta as Space: SB pp. 57, 59, 79. State-complete (sthitipurn) / state-dynamic (sthitishil): SB pp. 50, 68–69. Transparence, permeability, and pervasiveness as what evidences satta as one indivisible reality: “The Omnipotence eternally present as omnipresence is an indivisible entity, because its reality is apparent as transparence, permeability and omnipresence.” (SB, p. 46); restated as omnipresent, eternal, ever-existent, transparent, and permeating: SB p. 160. Permeating in insentient and sentient units and transparent in mutuality: MVD p. 32; the connection with images and recognition: PS p. 114.

passages.heading: references
passages.text: §1.2. Saturated (samprikt) — soaked, submerged, surrounded: SB pp. 48–49. Permeability as the ground of saturation, and the source’s connection to non-annihilation: “Being soaked itself is forcefulness. It becomes clear that units are soaked because Omnipotence is permeating. No matter how many times we divide a unit, each fragment remains submerged, surrounded, and soaked. It also becomes clear that a unit cannot be annihilated.” (SB, p. 57). The three aspects taken together, with permeativeness inferred from soakedness: SB p. 243. Surroundedness as what establishes regulation: “This very surroundedness itself clarifies the regulation of every unit, because every unit … remains regulated within a definite distance from one another, which itself is formless existence.” (SB, p. 79). Endowment chain (soaked → energy → force / magnetic force → recognition → orderliness): SB pp. 57, 61–62; KD 3.1. Recognition endowment: “Nature is recognisable in the state-complete Omnipotence with its countless unitness. Consequently, a provision for one unit to recognise another got manifest in existence.” (SB, p. 50); complementarity given in the bond: SB pp. 49–50, 53; bounded plurality provisions recognition: SB pp. 50, 57, 62; capacity (kshamata), ability (yogyata), receptivity (patrata): SB pp. 57, 62, 79; MVD p. 62; “transparent in mutuality”: MVD p. 32. Activeness endowment (forcefulness as force-side name of the same bond): “Every unit in its atomic state is active as orderliness, because it has inherent energy due to being saturated in Omnipotence.” (SB, p. 69); “Unit + Energy fullness = Activeness.” (SB, p. 69) — the Hindi term is ikaitva, unit-ness, which the translation renders as bare “Unit”; “Thus, without basic impulsion, the energy remains unmanifest, and without the energy, there is no basic impulsion.” (SB, p. 62); “Without absolute energy, there is no basic impulsion in matter, and without matter, absolute energy is not revealed. Nature is eternally present in absolute energy.” (MVD, p. 40); activeness as testimony of permeativeness: MVD p. 32; JV p. 150; forcefulness and basic impulsion endowed: SB p. 57; activeness always with contact in mutuality: SB p. 62; effort–motion–result (shram–gati–parinam): “Since nature is eternally active within existence, every activity has inseparable effort, motion and result.” (SB, p. 53); also SB pp. 58, 69; MVD p. 40. Regulation endowment: MVD p. 26; SB p. 57. Saturation itself as knowledge: “Saturated (samprikt): – Insentient and sentient nature is submerged, soaked and surrounded in Omnipotence. This itself is coexistence, coexistence itself is eternal, and this itself is knowledge. Law, regulation, balance, justice, dharma and ultimate truth are evident in coexistence only.” (MVD, pp. 32–33). Completeness drive grounded in the endowments; conducive environments and naturalness: SB pp. 50–51. Overlapping saturation descriptions: SB p. 57 links soakedness with forcefulness, submersion with activeness, and surroundedness with regulation; PS p. 114 links soakedness with energy-endowment, submersion with mutual recognition, and surroundedness with regulation. Permeation by state-complete satta as the ground of force-endowment, activeness, and manifestness: AVD pp. 115–116; force-endowment in saturation as the root of manifestness: SB p. 248. Image as the basis of mutual recognition: PS p. 121; imaging and influence in insentient mutuality: SB pp. 248–249.

passages.heading: references
passages.text: §1.3. Four aspects (form / roop, properties / guna, essential nature / svabhav, dharma): MVD pp. 11, 47, 50–51, 112. Three complementary truths (vastugat, vastu-sthiti, sthiti satya): SB pp. 250–251; YAT; MVD pp. 88, 97. Effort, motion, and result related to the four aspects, with overlapping correspondences: SB pp. 60–62. MVD p. 47 defines guna as relative powers and as the effect arising when more than one entity comes together, svabhav as essentiality and the usefulness of properties, and dharma as innateness. Bearer (guni) and property are inseparable; force is the property-endowed bearer and power is property: SB pp. 256–257. Form as shape, volume, and density and as the unit’s boundary-framework: SB pp. 249–250. Structural differentiation is stated concretely: atomic kind, state, and measure vary with nuclear and orbital particle number (MVD p. 42); form and properties change as an atom develops (SB p. 55); the motion-path reveals constitution and shape (SB p. 71); and particle-number changes produce qualitative changes until constitutional completeness (SB p. 86). A definite-proportion compound exhibits new conduct rather than merely retaining its constituents’ conducts: MVD p. 42. Imaging and light (prakash): MVD p. 45; the unit (bimb), its image (pratibimb), and imaging (pratibimban): PS pp. 121, 135. Being manifest with all four aspects: PS p. 119. The radiance-and-image discussion treats imaging as evidence of mutual recognition and distinguishes it from the influences of properties; it extends to animal recognition of essential nature and human exchange of values and evaluation of dharma: SB pp. 248–252. Imaging as indispensable to mutual manifestation and its distinction from motion or pressure: SB pp. 251–252. Essentiality manifest, communicated, and expressed according to state, motion, plane, and order: SB p. 179; all units’ expressions as activity saturated in Omnipresence: MVD p. 109. Sentient jeevan manifesting and communicating through a body: SB p. 52; its forces and powers as active and manifest: SB p. 63; communication and expression of human capacity, ability, and receptivity during awakening as manifestness: SB p. 66. Atom as root quantity with the four aspects: KD 3.9–3.10. The texts do not supply a quantitative particle-configuration derivation of every higher-order svabhav or dharma; the paper therefore keeps that order-specific content at the level of taught ontology. Companion facts: “Each unit is a whole along with its environment.” (SB, p. 13); “Each unit is orderliness with its ness and participates in overall orderliness.” (SB, p. 13); “Each unit moves towards ‘development’ in its natural state and ‘decline’ in its excited state.” (SB, p. 14). Unit + environment signifies continuity: SB p. 51; ness shown through essential nature in natural state: SB p. 54. Natural/excited state: SB pp. 14–15; reinstatement of natural motion (svabhav gati) after give and take: SB p. 59. Recognition and fulfilment within an atom: SB p. 123; endeavour with/against innateness: MVD p. 112. Peepal tree: JV p. 113. Harmony of the four aspects as essence of coexistence: MVD p. 21.

passages.heading: references
passages.text: §1.4. Supreme cause (mahakaran) in the sustaining sense: MVD pp. 288–289; SB pp. 49, 62. Time (kaal) as reckoning of activity’s duration: SB p. 251; fuller comparison in Nature of Time. Coexistence conservation; no arising from non-being (abhava); world perpetual (jagat satat): “Brahma is truth, the world is perpetual.” (MVD, p. 13). The specific argument for jeevan persistence belongs to §§1.7.1 and 1.9 (MVD p. 91; JV p. 20).

passages.heading: references
passages.text: §1.5. Inclination toward coexistence: “Everywhere, there exists a natural inclination towards coexistence. This inclination is what leads atomic particles to assemble into atoms, atoms to combine into molecules, and molecules to combine into molecular forms.” (JV, p. 67). Persist-or-decline: SB p. 14. Composition retains its dependence on constituents: “Whatever a basic entity is constituted of, it remains equal to that basic entity.” (SB, p. 260), with the soil example and “Change alone is recognised as development or decline” on the same page; the human body as of the order of the pranic cell: SB p. 262; restated for formations however vast: SB p. 264; the Earth entire as of the order of its constituent atoms, molecules, and cells: SB p. 265. Material manifestation as the pranic order and reversion to material constituents: SB pp. 75–77. This scopes the composition claim to insentient nature rather than forbidding every change of order. Mixture (mishran) and compound (yaugik): MVD p. 42. Transmission of composition method (rachna vidhi) by constitution, seed, lineage, education-sanskar: JV pp. 48, 82; MVD pp. 92–93.

passages.heading: references
passages.text: §1.6. Four orders (padarth, pran, jeev, gyan avasthas); cumulative dharmas: SB p. 179; MVD p. 115. Order table (essential natures and dharmas — sangathan–vighatan/astitva; sarak–marak/pushti; cruel–uncruel/jeene ki aasha; six human values/sukh): SB p. 179; JV p. 44. SB Ch. 9 identifies vitalising–devitalising relative to bodily nourishment and protection, cruelty as suffering caused to another, and humane essential nature through its expression in awakening. Animal and knowledge orders have brains, while the nervous system is fully enriched only in the human body: MVD pp. 83, 93; JV p. 59. Five koshas and their distribution across the orders: MVD pp. 49–50. Existence stable, development definite: MVD p. 5. Existential progression (niyati-kram): MVD pp. 8, 13 . Reversion of biological to material order: SB pp. 76–78. Way of existence (niyati-vidhi) and conformance modes: SB pp. 62–63 (animal-order adhyasa as gestational inheritance of conduct-pattern; homonym caution vs Advaita’s adhyasa, §5.7.5). Statuses within matter and designed completeness stages: SB pp. 50–52, 78. Modes of manifestation per order; countlessness as practical uncountability: MVD p. 289; SB p. 49.

passages.heading: references
passages.text: §1.6.1. Self-regulating saturated units (swatah-saspurt); mediative (madhyasth) regulation: SB p. 57; MVD p. 26. “Regulation itself becomes clear in the form of law. Consequently, there is provision in every unit for recognising one another based on law. This itself is the meaning of regulation.” (SB, p. 57). “Omnipotence is mediative, therefore the nature saturated in it is regulated and conserved. The nucleus within every atom is the mediative activity, whereby the atom’s generative-degenerative activities and relative powers are regulated and conserved.” (MVD, p. 26). Conformance modes per order (niyati-vidhi): §1.6 references; animal adhyasa: SB pp. 62–63. Sanskar-conformance: SB pp. 62–63. The human development of this account and its sources are given under §1.13.3.

passages.heading: references
passages.text: §§1.7, 1.11. Span of the drive: “The nature saturated in the state-complete Omnipotence is oriented for development and awakening until realisation in Omnipotence. Development refers to constitutional completeness, activity completeness, and conduct completeness, along with their continuity. Awakening refers to resolution and authenticity.” (SB, p. 51). Existential-truth bound (nature bound for development until realised in Omnipotence; applies to insentient and sentient): SB p. 91. Two developments that must not be collapsed (compositional progression vs development in the atom; three stages scoped to the constitutionally complete jeevan atom): KD 3.2–3.3. Happiness→bliss as knowledge-order / sentient face of the same drive (felt ladder in §1.9; terminus as realisation in §1.14): JV p. 138; MVD p. 101; SB p. 51. Two atomic paths and projection/reflection: SB p. 60. Triad joint structure: “Every physical-chemical activity is an inseparable presence of effort, motion and result. Each of these is a joint form of the other two.” (SB, p. 58); sodium–chlorine illustration: SB p. 58. Internal unfolding chain: “Saturation in uniform energy itself is forcefulness, forcefulness itself is basic impulsion, basic impulsion itself is activity, activity itself is effort-motion-result, effort-motion-result itself is development and its continuity.” (SB, p. 62). Force in state, power in motion: SB pp. 248, 256–257. Teleological goals: “In the sentient atom: Conduct completeness is in the form of destination of motion. Activity completeness is in the form of restfulness of effort. Constitutional completeness (the jeevan atom) is in the form of immortality of result.” (SB, p. 58); “The result is meant to attain the goal of immortality, the effort is meant to attain the goal of restfulness, motion is meant to attain the goal of destination. This goal itself becomes evident in the form of development progression and development.” (SB, p. 71); “…at the core of effort, motion and result, the study of immortality of result, restfulness of effort, and final-destination of motion is necessary…” (MVD, p. 104). Hindi terms for the transitions: gathanpurnata, kriyapurnata, acharanpurnata; goals: parinam ki amarta, shram ka vishram, gati ka gantavya.

passages.heading: references
passages.text: §1.7.1. Sentience threshold at atomic level: SB pp. 52, 92. Integration through hungry/undigested (overfull) complementarity: MVD p. 8; SB pp. 58, 71; KD 3.3 (hungry, undigested, satisfied; inexhaustible force). Closed particle constitution: SB p. 55. Qualitative change tied to quantitative change in matter, and the separation of the two at completeness: SB p. 86. Crossing evidence: “An evolving-constitution atom is with molecular-bondage and weight-bondage. However, when the contraction and expansion activity increases in this atom, it instantly breaks free from its group and attains constitutional completeness, becoming a jeevan atom. The evidence of constitutional completeness is the jeevan atom’s liberation from molecular-bondage and weight-bondage, and its having the hope-bondage.” (MVD, p. 91); also SB p. 114. Immortality of result evident as sentient jeevan: SB p. 59. Recognition upgraded to inner circuit: “…the recognition of taste, which could not become manifest in insentient nature, first became manifest in sentient nature. In sentient nature, the strength of mun expresses itself in the form of hope-power. Its activities are selection and taste-recognition.” (SB, pp. 80–81).

passages.heading: references
passages.text: §1.8. Jeevan as constitutionally complete sentient atom; knower is jeevan, not body; knower as seer in seer–doer–enjoyer triad: MVD p. 115; SB pp. 91–92; KD 3.18. Five aspects in the jeevan-cloud: MVD p. 13. Faculties and characteristic powers distinguished: SB p. 63; five insentient forces and sentient powers: SB pp. 84–85. Orbital structure: “The nucleus of the sentient unit (a constitutionally complete atom) is referred to as atma. The particles in its first orbit are referred to as buddhi, those in the second orbit are referred to as chitta, those in the third orbit are referred to as vritti, and those in the fourth orbit are referred to as mun.” (MVD, p. 78). Ten activities: JV pp. 73–74, 92–94. Equal capacity of jeevan in every human through inexhaustible strengths and powers: SB p. 91. JV states both that every jeevan continuously operates through ten activities and that, in delusion, only four and a half are effective; awakening joins recognising and fulfilling to knowing and believing. The root of delusion is identifying jeevan with the body: JV pp. 93–94; SB pp. 91–92. Sensitivity (sanvedansheelta) and cognisance (sangyansheelta) are balanced rather than opposed; cognisance regulates sensory activity in awakening: SB p. 64; MVD pp. 274–275. The body as medium and medhas as receiver of jeevan’s signals: MVD pp. 82–83; the fully enriched nervous system only in the human body: MVD p. 93; JV p. 59. Projection–reflection (KD 3.12) and force/power as state–motion of the same faculties (KD 3.6, 3.8; printed p. 84) — not a second five-fold list. Koshas (annamaya, pranamaya/pran kosha, manomaya, anandamaya, vigyanmaya): MVD pp. 49–50; their distribution across orders is explained in §1.6. Study circuit (reflection): “Affirmation of truth in the form of coexistence through the way of study is referred to as ratiocination in mun (in the form of acceptance), deliberation in vritti (by way of qualitative analysis), direct recognition in chitta, and enlightenment in buddhi.” (MVD, p. 126); termination in atma-bodh and realisation: MVD pp. 286–287. Projection as evidencing cascade; knowledge unfolding (gyan udghatan): MVD pp. 99–100. “I” and “mine” on the delusional plane: MVD p. 78. Animal-order partial expression: MVD pp. 82, 278. Three statuses of buddhi: MVD pp. 278–279. The ten enumerated in finer grain as named positions at each faculty, each position pairing what is borne in state with what carries it outward: MVD pp. 328–348; AVD pp. 91–94. Higher- and lower-conformance (purvanukram, paranukram): MVD pp. 207–208. Projection of realisation through authenticity, resolve, visualisation, analysis, and selection: the outward column of the §1.8 table; KD 3.6, 3.12. Tasting forms ruchi-mulak, mulya-mulak, and lakshya-mulak: PS pp. 40–41; MVD pp. 124, 203, 343, 346; JV pp. 138–140; developed in Axiology: Value Theory §1.2. This study renders the reflective activity of buddhi as comprehension (bodh) and of chitta as direct apprehension (sakshatkar), while the MVD English of p. 126 prints “enlightenment” and “direct recognition.” Six perspectives and restricted deliberation: MVD p. 67; JV p. 73. The driver–body illustration follows JV p. 94.

passages.heading: references
passages.text: §1.9. Felt form of the happiness→bliss face of the completeness drive (§1.11). Jeevan values as harmonies: “Among the values, jeevan values are known by the names — happiness, peace, contentment and bliss, which are only names of the state of harmony within jeevan. Happiness is when there is harmony in mun and vritti, peace is when there is harmony in vritti and chitta, contentment is when there is harmony in chitta and buddhi, and bliss is when there is harmony in buddhi and atma.” (JV, p. 138). Four stages of happiness: “Happiness, peace, contentment and bliss - these are four stages of happiness.” (MVD, p. 163). Alignment with societal goals: JV p. 61 (§1.15). Placement of the four values as named activities borne at mun, vritti, chitta, and buddhi, with peace defined at vritti as absence of resistance between desire and thought: MVD pp. 328–346. Ultimate bliss (paramanand) at realised atma, and the effects of atma realised in truth on the remaining faculties: MVD pp. 100–101. Channelling of energies: “The mode of channelling jeevan’s energies towards development (awakening) is through curiosity in mun, enthusiasm in vritti, delight in chitta, elation and immersion in buddhi, and finally, realisation in atma. For this, inward regulation of jeevan energies is essential.” (MVD, p. 77). Projection–reflection spiral (understand / make understood; widening evidence “today… one issue, tomorrow… two”): working English of KD 3.12 — attributed paraphrase; verify against Hindi before quotation. Human- and jeevan-aspiration meaningful together when projection is consistent: KD 3.12 (working English). Inward regulation; mediative atma disciplines faculties and body: MVD p. 277; nucleus/atma same structural role at two scales: MVD pp. 26, 78. Persistence: “Jeevan continues to exist even after death as it does while driving a body.” (JV, p. 20). Reassociation with another body is stated in JV, PDF p. 55 (printed p. 54). Cumulative resolution–prosperity–fearlessness–coexistence correspondence: KD §3.12, printed p. 112.

passages.heading: references
passages.text: §1.10. Kriyā as activity throughout nature, distinguished from karma as activity together with aspiration; karma in the narrow sense as the doing (middle term of desire–karma–result); five limbs (doer, cause, objective, result, effect) as the structure of an intentional act for checking balance; balance of desire, karma, and result as accomplishment of the desire: working English of KD Ch. 1 (printed pp. 1–2) — attributed paraphrase; verify against Hindi page images before quotation. Enactment / living proof: §§1.11.2, 1.16. Deluded vs awakened freedom in performing and undergoing action: “Deluded humans are independent when performing actions, but dependent when experiencing the consequences of those actions. Awakened humans are independent both in performing actions and in experiencing their consequences.” (MVD, p. 15); KD Ch. 1 parallel (working English). Prarabdha as results remaining to be undergone: MVD p. 91.

passages.heading: references
passages.text: §1.11.1. Restfulness of effort; realisation (anubhav) and absolute resolution (samadhan) on the deific plane: SB p. 51; the §§1.7, 1.11 reference entry above. “Absence of delusion itself is restfulness” (nirbhramta hi vishram): MVD, Ch. 5. Epistemic stall — body mistaken for jeevan: SB p. 91. Seer–doer–enjoyer (drashta–karta–bhokta); delusion as doer and enjoyer without seer; projection–reflection as T2 path: KD 3.12, 3.18.

passages.heading: references
passages.text: §1.11.2. Destination of motion; authentic conduct and living proof (pramanikta) in universal orderliness (vyavastha), mutual satisfaction and justice: MVD p. 80. Individual and social completeness distinguished: MVD pp. 15–16. Perceiver status (drishta pad) evidenced in orderliness with ness and living proof: SB pp. 137–138, 159. Seer, doer, and enjoyer together in awakened tradition; projection as living proof: KD 3.12, 3.18.

passages.heading: references
passages.text: §§1.12, 1.12.1. Terms for order and development — niyati-kram, niyati-vidhi, vikas-kram, jagriti-kram: MVD pp. 13–14 (first two named in Paribhasha Samhita). Pranic→animal junction — bodily basis from order chain, sentient unit from constitutional completeness: MVD pp. 8, 13, 91; SB pp. 76–77. Sentient-mode mapping of triad to goals: SB pp. 58, 71; projection/reflection toward resolution: SB pp. 60, 64–65, 69.

passages.heading: references
passages.text: §1.12.2. Plane (pad) as developmental standing; four planes; order–plane non-alignment; padmukti as release from planes in the complete condition: SB p. 52. Five human types (pashu-manav, rakshas-manav, discerning human, dev-manav, divya-manav): MVD p. 160. Human body as enabling medium with enriched nervous system and imagination: MVD p. 115; JV pp. 79, 93.

passages.heading: references
passages.text: §1.13.1. “Nothing is isolated – that is the principle.” (JV, p. 43). Complementarity actualised as value in mutuality: SB p. 53. Relationship vs contact: “the mutuality where expectations are predetermined in the sense of completeness” vs “the mutuality where expectations are voluntary” (MVD, pp. 61–62). Justice and injustice immediately apply in contact; duties concern contacts as well as relationships: MVD pp. 61, 311–312. Essentiality as value: “Entire beingness implies the essentiality of units in every plane and order. Essentiality refers to value… It is values that are reciprocated and mutually recognised, as complementarity, mutual recognition, and impression occur only in mutuality.” (SB, p. 50). Thirty values (tees mulya) as four jeevan, six human, nine established, nine expressed, and two object values: Paribhasha pp. 151, 154. MVD p. 305 names jeevan, human, established, civic (shishta), and usefulness-and-art value families; this study reads shishta as the expressed pair of the established values (Editorial Notes). JV p. 43 repeats human, jeevan, established, civic, and usefulness values; JV pp. 137–138 distinguishes object values, the four jeevan values, and relationship values. PS pp. 151, 154 provides the explicit thirty-value enumeration; MAD reader p. 30 explicitly names the principal nine established values and their corresponding expressions. Humane and higher-humane essential natures: MVD pp. 50–60. Recognition and fulfilment: “Every entity of nature recognises another; that is why it fulfils. An atomic particle too recognises another, and as a result, these particles abide in orderliness.” (JV, p. 69). Capacity, ability, receptivity developed through environment and interference: SB p. 61. Use, right-use, purposeful-use: MVD p. 27. Seed and naturalness: SB p. 54. Realisation in coexistence as fulfilment made evident: SB p. 51. An illustrative enumeration of the nine established values: JV p. 108; direct principal classification: MAD reader p. 30. Named values defined within the appendix of jeevan’s activities, each set at a faculty beside the term through which it is expressed: MVD pp. 328–348; tabulated entries: AVD pp. 91–94, with state/motion orientation checked against KD §3.8, printed p. 84. Values do not flow where relationships are not recognised: JV p. 55.

passages.heading: references
passages.text: §1.13.2. Selection and taste-recognition in sentient nature: SB pp. 80–81; animal-order jeevan operates within hope-bound activity, while human evaluation is articulated through six perspectives. “All human behaviour is manifest in six perspectives: – (1) pleasant-unpleasant, (2) healthy-unhealthy, (3) profit-loss, (4) justice-injustice, (5) dharma-adharma, and (6) truth-untruth.” (MVD, p. 67). “The behaviour of humans with inhumane perspective is in the refuge of pleasant-unpleasant, healthy-unhealthy, and profit-loss. The behaviour of humans with humane perspective is in the refuge of justice-injustice, dharma-adharma, and truth-untruth.” (MVD, p. 67). Humane refuge reorganisation: MVD pp. 27, 67. Domain regulation: “The regulation of human behaviour takes place through justice, discipline in thoughts takes place through dharma, and realisation takes place only through truth.” (MVD, p. 137). Graduated chain: “The law itself is justice, justice itself is dharma, dharma itself is truth, truth itself is abundance (coexistence), realisation of abundance itself is bliss, bliss itself is jeevan, and law is in jeevan.” (MVD, p. 15); also MVD p. 162; KD vikalp / Ch. 1 parallel (working English). Hindi perspective terms: priya–apriya, hita–ahita, labh–alabh, nyaya–anyaya, dharma–adharma, satya–asatya.

passages.heading: references
passages.text: §1.13.3. Knowledge–law–regulation–balance–justice–dharma–truth: MVD p. 174. Statutory law as institutional codification: MVD p. 311. “Recognising relationships, fulfilling values, evaluating, and achieving mutual satisfaction is justice.” (MVD, p. 311). Value, character, and ethics as the account of humane conduct: PS p. 151. Value-flow depends on recognising relationships: JV p. 55. The caregiver illustration is this study’s application. Human happiness and relationship-values provide the normative premises: MVD pp. 50–51, 61–62, 67. Family and social assemblies as continuity through relationships: the composition comparison draws on JV pp. 48, 67, 82 and MVD pp. 92–93; social continuity is developed in §1.15.

passages.heading: references
passages.text: §1.14. “The goal of development is for nature, saturated in Omnipotence, to be realised in Omnipotence. Realisation itself is the form of awakening. It is only through awakening that there is the orderliness of recognition and fulfilment. Recognition and fulfilment themselves constitute authenticity; this is the expression of realisation.” (SB, p. 81). Verity chain — “truth itself is abundance (coexistence), realisation of abundance itself is bliss, bliss itself is jeevan”: MVD pp. 14–15. Bliss evidenced in living: JV p. 61. The threefold content of knowledge — holistic view of coexistence, knowledge of jeevan, and knowledge of humane conduct — is stated in SB p. 116 and MVD p. 126. KD distinguishes the roles: jeevan is knower and seer, existence-as-coexistence is the known and seen, and the threefold content is knowledge (KD 3.17–3.18). The roles become harmonised in awakening without erasing their distinctions. Gyan as a name for actionless pervasive reality: MVD p. 35; vivek and vigyan as recognition of goals and determination of direction for their accomplishment: MVD p. 170. Presentation, communication, and expression in awakened human living: PS pp. 22, 119, 206; their joint realisation-based use: MVD p. 328; realised understanding expressed, communicated, and made manifest in human tradition: AVD pp. 115–116. Form activity, word activity, and communication as understanding and enabling understanding: MVD pp. 109–110. Art as making qualities evident and expression meaningful, joining usefulness and beauty: PS p. 56. Gross compositions, subtle atoms, causal atma, and supreme cause satta: MVD pp. 288–289.

passages.heading: references
passages.text: §1.15. Four human goals — resolution (samadhan), prosperity (samridhi), fearlessness (abhay), coexistence (saha-astitva). Alignment with jeevan values (points to §1.9 table): “Resolution = Happiness. We realise happiness wherever we are resolved… Thereafter, we realise peace while evidencing resolution and prosperity in the family. We realise contentment by living orderly in society. We realise bliss in the course of evidencing our understanding.” (JV, p. 61). Undivided society (akhand samaj), universal orderliness (sarvabhaum vyavastha); five dimensions and their functions — education-character (shiksha-sanskar), justice-preservation (nyaya-suraksha), health-restraint (swasthya-sanyam), production-work (utpadan-karya), exchange-storage (vinimay-kosh): MVD pp. 259–260; humane tradition (manav parampara). Individual and social completeness distinguished: MVD pp. 15–16.

passages.heading: references
passages.text: §1.16. The evidence distinctions assemble the preceding account of study, realisation, practice, and humane conduct; see §§1.11.2, 1.10, 1.14 references. They distinguish MD’s warrant from independent public identification of its proposed sentient unit.

passages.heading: references
passages.text: Advaita Vedanta (§2)

passages.heading: references
passages.text: The primary texts below are read with the cited commentaries. Verse and sutra identifiers are the principal locators; PDF positions refer to the linked editions.

passages.heading: references
passages.text: CU — Chandogya Upanishad, with Shankara’s commentary, trans. Swami Gambhirananda. Cited: 6.2.1–6.2.2 for existence and rejection of origination from non-being (§2.1); 6.1.4 for the clay teaching (§2.5); 6.8.7 for tat tvam asi (§2.9).

passages.heading: references
passages.text: TU — Taittiriya Upanishad in Eight Upanishads, Vol. 1, with Shankara’s commentary, trans. Swami Gambhirananda. Cited: 2.1.1 and commentary for satyam–jnanam–anantam (quotation at PDF p. 210); 2.5 for the bliss sheath; 2.7 for Brahman as rasa (§2.2).
